title: Cowboys GTA Rewind: What Was Dallas’ Record For Every GTA Release
full_text:
On Thursday night, another week of NFL action kicks into full swing , but that's not the main headline. Most people are eagerly waiting for the midnight drop of Grand Theft Auto VI , which has been 13 years in the making.
Unfortunately for Cowboys Nation, that could spell doom.
The last time the Cowboys won a Super Bowl, as we all know, came in 1996 in Super Bowl XXX over the Pittsburgh Steelers. The team has been on a highly-publicized Super Bowl drought since then. The following year, the first Grand Theft Auto title was released.
In the years a new GTA title gets released, the Cowboys have had some of their worst seasons of the past 30 years. There have been eight GTA titles and only one playoff appearance, so let's hope that the team can buck the trend this season, even though we know it won't be easy.
A look at the Cowboys' struggles in every year that a Grand Theft Auto title was released can be seen below.
As history shows, Grand Theft Auto releases have not been kind to the Cowboys. To be fair, the past 30 years haven't been, either. Dallas has made the playoffs only once since the initial Grand Theft Auto was released, with zero playoff wins.
Maybe we can blame the Grand Theft Auto franchise for the Cowboys' Super Bowl drought. Does anyone think Jerry Jones is secretly a fan and that's where all his attention has been when he's not focused on drilling more oil wells? These are the important questions that need to be asked.
GTA 6 will officially drop at midnight local time in your area (unless you live in Hawaii, then it drops at 7:00 p.m. HT, which is midnight ET, so you get to live in paradise and skip and the queue. Happy gaming, everyone.

title: Dallas Cowboys Week 11 Injury Report: Jalen Thompson Returns, DaRon Bland Among 7 Out
full_text:
The Dallas Cowboys returned to the practice field for the first time since announcing that defensive coordinator Christian Parker has been stripped of play-calling duties . The announcement comes as the team prepares to face off against the Tennessee Titans at AT&T Stadium in Week 11 , in an effort to get back into the win column.
Dallas enters the week as heavy favorites against the 1-8 Titans, so it's a perfect time to salvage the season that will be on life support if they suffer another embarrassing loss at home.
With the team returning to practice, we got our first injury report of the week, which had a mix of good and bad news. The good news: starting safety Jalen Thompson practiced for the first time since he was injured in Week 3, after the team activated his 21-day practice window.

title: How Dallas Cowboys Botched Christian Parker's Tenure, From Hiring to Demotion
full_text:
The Dallas Cowboys have made a huge change on the defensive side of the ball ahead of the Week 11 contest against the Tennessee Titans.
According to ESPN's Kimberley A. Martin , Adam Schefter and Todd Archer, the Cowboys are stripping defensive coordinator Christian Parker of his play-calling duties and are handing them over to senior defensive assistant Mike Pettine.
The writing was on the wall on Tuesday that this would happen after owner Jerry Jones admitted for the first time that the Cowboys were at least considering a change with Parker, something he has never come close to saying.
While this is the right move after how bad the Cowboys' defense has been this season, it doesn't erase the fact that the Cowboys made this a much messier situation than it needed to be.
Hindsight is always 20/20, of course, but seeing the results now is not the only reason why we can say the Cowboys shouldn't have hired Parker in the first place.
The Cowboys have made it quite clear there is an elevated sense of urgency this season, and for a few reasons.
Dallas hasn't made the playoffs in the past two seasons, Dak Prescott is getting up there in age, and even Jerry Jones has admitted he doesn't have much time left on this Earth to win another Super Bowl.
"I have a natural urgency because of my age. My immediate tomorrows are a big thing to me," he explained . "I am supremely responsible for where we are right now. There is no question about that. I accept that. That doesn't deter me from wanting to get it done and get it done now this year."
By all accounts, the Cowboys were definitely in win-now mode.
So, hiring a first-time defensive coordinator just didn't make sense. Even the Cowboys admitted they figured there would be growing pains, something Jones has said time and time again amid the defensive struggles this season.
If the team didn't have the time to go through those growing pains, why would it hire a rookie play-caller to begin with? This is just a case of the Cowboys setting Parker up to fail.
This one also falls on head coach Brian Schottenheimer, who was very involved in the process of hiring a new defensive coordinator and pushed for Parker to be hired. Don't let Schottenheimer escape liability for this mess.
When the Cowboys hired Pettine as a senior defensive assistant, it was the right move, but it was also a clear indictment on Parker and wasn't a good look for him.
Making the whole situation worse was the fact that Pettine reported directly Schottenheimer , which gave the indication Pettine was above the guy he was supposedly coming in to help.
Of course, the Cowboys tried to downplay all of that, from the hire being an indictment on Parker to the reporting structure being a bad look for Parker, but nobody bought what the Cowboys were selling.
One of the ways the Cowboys tried to downplay it was to say that it was in the plans to hire Pettine as a consultant in the first place, he just wasn't available initially.
If that was the case, the Cowboys should have hired someone else before the season to give Parker an experienced defensive play-caller to bounce ideas off of.
Not only would that have been the right move to make after hiring a first-time defensive coordinator, it would have avoided the kind of negative optics the in-season hiring of Pettine provided.
Again, we believe the Cowboys made the right move here with the decision to go from Parker to Pettine as the play-caller because something had to give. But, again, this is another situation the Cowboys made messier than it should have been.
For starters, Schottenheimer had clearly changed his tune on Parker after the Week 10 loss by failing to clearly commit to his hand-picked defensive coordinator.
Then, there was Jones' aforementioned comment about the team considering a change with Parker's duties, something he did not need to admit publicly but did anyway.
The last step in this months-long humiliation ritual is the Cowboys keeping Parker on as the defensive coordinator and not firing him. To be quite frank, we're shocked Parker didn't resign, but that may have more to do with his contract and/or pride than his desire to remain in Dallas.
The more merciful thing to do would have been to fire Parker and let him move on. Instead, Parker has to walk around the building and roam the sidelines with everyone knowing he has no real power anymore despite still having his title.
Again, none of this is to say that Parker is blameless in the team's struggles on defense this season. This is more about how poorly Dallas has handled the entire process, from start to finish.

title: Cowboys' Schottenheimer Addresses Christian Parker's Future With Team
full_text:
On Wednesday, the Dallas Cowboys announced that they would be making a major change on the defensive side of the ball. Following yet another frustrating performance, they decided to strip defensive coordinator Christian Parker of his play-calling duties, giving the job to senior defensive assistant Mike Pettine.
The move puts Parker in a difficult spot as he's still technically the defensive coordinator, but his future doesn't look good. Cowboys On SI's Josh Sanchez wrote that Parker is being strung along at this point , saying there's no reason for him to stay without the full duties of a defensive coordinator.
Head coach Brian Schottenheimer doesn't seem to feel the same way. He spoke with reporters on Wednesday afternoon and claimed that Parker is still a critical piece of the staff. He also reiterated that Parker still has a bright future .
“I want to clarify a couple of things right off the bat. Christian Parker is still our defensive coordinator and he is still a critical piece of what we’re trying to do as we search for answers and solutions. I think he has an incredibly bright future, not just this year, but beyond with us," Schottenheimer said.
Coach Schotty added that the decision was made on Tuesday and that it was ultimately he choice. He also said he and Parker had some honest conversations, saying the defensive coordinator understands and is focused on beating the Tennessee Titans this weekend.
“I think Christian is an incredibly strong and committed man who wants to get it right. I love that we can have the honest conversations. At the end of the day, this decision was made because I think it gives us the best chance to win. CP understands the decision that was made, and he wants to help us beat the Titans,” Schottenheimer said .
As for the play-calling duties for the rest of the season, Schottenheimer confirmed that this weekend isn't a test run. Instead, Pettine will be the play-caller for the remainder of the season. He was asked if this move will be considered a failure if Dallas misses the playoffs, and the head coach said this entire season would be considered a failure if that's how it ends.
“If we don’t make the playoffs, it’s a failure. The season is a failure. We play to win. We have seven games left, and we need to find a run of success,” Schottenheimer.
For Schottenheimer, the real question is when he will be held accountable. This is the second defensive coordinator after Matt Eberflus in 2025 to take the blame for the team's failures. Eventually, the Cowboys need to look at the man in charge of the whole team and realize the problem starts at the top.

title: Christian Parker Now Lame Duck Defensive Coordinator, NFL History Shows
full_text:
The Dallas Cowboys have been looking for a scapegoat after failing to live up to expectations through the first half of the season, and they finally found one in defensive coordinator Christian Parker .
On Wednesday morning, just two days after head coach Brian Schottenheimer failed to give Parker a vote of confidence , it was reported that the team stripped the first-time DC of his play-calling duties . Now, the question everyone is asking is, "What's next?" for Parker's long-term future in Dallas.
Conventional wisdom would tell you this is the nail in the coffin for Parker, and the team will likely move on at the end of the season and search for a new defensive coordinator , marking the fifth change at the position in the past five years.
In fact, NFL history backs up the thought that Parker is now a lame duck defensive coordinator, much like the recent examples of men in his situation who also had their play-calling stripped in the middle of the season.
We can all see how the next chapter of this story plays out. The Cowboys will either move on from Parker after another lost season, or Parker will walk away after being undermined and having his play-calling duties stripped.
There is no reason for Parker to return as "defensive coordinator" if he has no defensive coordinator responsibilities. And as recent NFL history shows, the most likely outcome is the team hiring a new defensive coordinator during the offseason, as Bobby Belt of 105.3 The Fan points out.
There is no need for the Cowboys to continue the charade for the rest of the season, because everyone can see the writing on the wall.
Dallas rolled the dice on an unproven, first-time defensive coordinator and it didn't work. The team bet on potential, and with the spotlight in Dallas, coaches aren't going to be afforded the grace and time to develop as a coach with Jerry Jones' expectations hanging over them.
That's the harsh reality of the Cowboys organization, and it's why Jones needs to open his wallet and pay for a coaching staff that has been around the league and understands what comes with leading America's Team. Whether it be Parker or Brian Schottenheimer, the "first-time" experiment has not worked out in Dallas.

title: Dallas Cowboys Desperate Defensive Change Is Indictment of Brian Schottenheimer
full_text:
The Dallas Cowboys made a desperate but necessary change on Wednesday morning, after failing to show any signs of improvement on defense and an embarrassing second-half collapse against the San Francisco 49ers in Week 10.
Defensive coordinator Christian Parker was stripped of play-calling duties , with senior defensive assistant and former NFL head coach Mike Pettine taking over play-calling moving forward .
While Parker fell on the sword after head coach Brian Schottenheimer threw him under the bus , you have to wonder what changes should be made next in Dallas. It's not fair that Parker is the only one catching heat for the team's failures.
It all starts at the top, and Dallas' main problem has been a lack of preparation. While Parker is the defensive coordinator, it ultimately falls on the head coach to ensure that the coaching staff and players are all prepared on game day. Schottenheimer has failed to do so. It's easy to blame Parker for the defense's continued struggles . It's equally as easy to blame Schottenheimer for the team's overall failures.
Dallas has fielded a putrid defense for the past two seasons. That's two miserable defenses with two different defensive coordinators. There has only been one constant: Brian Schottenheimer as head coach.
At the end of the day, it's on Schottenheimer to make sure everyone is prepared and in the right position to succeed. That has never been done. Like Parker, Schottenheimer seems to be in over his head and has shown an unwillingness to alter his strategies.
If the head coach is okay with getting stagnant with his game plan, why wouldn't the defensive coordinator follow? Now that Parker has been thrown under the bus , it's all on Schottenheimer to turn things around.
If nothing changes in Dallas with Pettine calling the plays, Schottenheimer should be the next domino to fall. The Cowboys are at a point where they need to strongly consider cleaning house, and if the team takes the next step of removing Parker as defensive coordinator after the season, the best move would be to hit the reset button and completely revamp the coaching staff.
Something needs to change, as Dak Prescott pointed out , and that something may just be the entire coaching staff.

title: Bo Nix Gets Candid About the Harsh Reality Facing Fernando Mendoza
full_text:
The Denver Broncos are about to face Fernando Mendoza for the first time, though it won't be the last.
Drafted No. 1 overall by the Las Vegas Raiders earlier this year, Mendoza is poised to make just his second career start against the Broncos on Sunday . The former Indiana Hoosiers National Champion and Heisman Winner had to face the Seattle Seahawks in his first-ever start last week, and while the rookie hung in there, the Raiders lost the game 21-13.
That's something Mendoza has in common with Bo Nix: both players' first-ever NFL starts came against Mike Macdonald's Seahawks defense. Much like Mendoza, Nix got his licks in against the Seahawks, rushing for a touchdown, but ultimately lost the game in Seattle , 26-20. Nix did get to balance the scales by defeating the Seahawks in Denver a few weeks back.
At least Mendoza got to start his first NFL game at home, though. The rookie didn't find the end zone as a passer against Seattle, but he did rush for a touchdown, just like Nix.
With Kirk Cousins traded to the Minnesota Vikings last week, the Mendoza era has officially begun in Vegas, and the Raiders aren't looking back. The Broncos can expect to see Mendoza twice per year for the foreseeable future.
Nix will make his 44th regular-season start on Sunday against the Raiders. Suffice it to say, Nix knows exactly what his Silver and Black counterpart is going through as a rookie starter, but he said it will get easier for Mendoza.
"It's night and day," Nix said on Wednesday. "It's hard for a rookie quarterback. I don't care if you're sitting behind a guy like Kirk [Cousins] who you can learn from, but you still have to go out there and ultimately play and ultimately do it. And so it's not easy. And to his credit, he played a really good defense last week. He's going to play a really good one this week."
Nix had to face Macdonald's Seahawks and Mike Tomlin's Pittsburgh Steelers to open up his NFL career two years ago. And nobody knows better than Nix: there's no way to make it an easier on a rookie quarterback. The only way out is through, so to speak, meaning a quarterback can only learn and develop by going through the refiner's fire.
"Unfortunately, the world's not going to give him any time to go through the obstacles that it takes as a rookie quarterback. But for him, he'll continue to develop," Nix said of Mendoza. "He's a smart kid, and he's played in big moments in college. I think that does translate, and he's going to work hard and continue to get better."
Mendoza seems to have a grit about him, but it's too early to say for sure how much his experience playing on the biggest college football stages will truly serve him as an NFL quarterback. Let's first see how the rookie fares against a Broncos defense that's ranked near the top of the league in sacks, and has a legitimate chance to three-peat as NFL sack champions.
"I would say, in my opinion, it gets easier," Nix said. "It's not always going to stay difficult, like he probably feels it is now."
Nix vs. Justin Herbert has been a great quarterback rivalry. Nix vs. Patrick Mahomes has been even better, as the Broncos and the Kansas City Chiefs vie for the AFC West crown.
On Sunday, Broncos and Raiders fans will be treated to the first iteration of Nix vs. Mendoza. Although the Raiders are 4-6, I'd caution against overlooking them; remember the brutality of their last trip to Mile High?
The Broncos narrowly escaped with a 10-7 win and it came at the cost of losing running back J.K. Dobbins for the season. Now, that was a different coaching staff with a different quarterback, but Klint Kubiak and Mendoza will be coming in hot, looking to upset the Broncos.
It doesn't appear as if Mendoza will have Pro Bowl tight end Brock Bowers , though. But that will only mean that Denver will have to lock in on Michael Mayer, Bowers's backup who is currently the fifth-highest-paid tight end in the NFL.
If Denver takes care of business, though, its AFC West record will climb to 3-1 this season, wresting  back the tiebreaker over the Chiefs for the divisional lead. The stakes are big for Denver, even with the Raiders being a sub-.500 team right now.
Expect Nix and company to handle their business against Mendoza and the Raiders. But it won't be easy.

title: Broncos' Injury Report Delivers Triple Dose of Good News
full_text:
The Denver Broncos just had their first practice since enjoying a well-earned bye .
The 7-2 Broncos are preparing to host the 4-6 Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday. Don't let the Raiders' schedule fool you; the Broncos are expecting a divisional rock-fight.
"The one thing that I've learned, noticed, and have witnessed myself is it doesn't matter what a team's record is when you're talking about divisional games because they're going to show up and play hard no matter what," Courtland Sutton said on Wednesday. "And the Raiders have always been that team. No matter what their record is, they always show up and play the Broncos really hard."
Be ready for anything. The Raiders are no longer led by Kirk Cousins, after he was traded to the Minnesota Vikings; it's rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza under center now. The Broncos will get their first-ever look at the No. 1 overall pick in the draft and former Heisman Trophy winner.
The bye week afforded some of Denver's injured players the opportunity to rest and recover. In the first practice report of Week 11, there are several encouraging developments and a couple of concerns we'll be monitoring over the next few days.
The big news is Lohner's return from the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) List. The Broncos started his clock today, buying themselves a 21-day window to decide whether to activate him.
If they don't activate Lohner, he'll be unavailable the rest of the season. If he is activated — and we should assume he will be — it'll be interesting to see how the Broncos juggle the roster math. At whose expense will Lohner's return be? Rookie tight end Dallen Bentley? Or it could be a player at another position.
Hufanga is back after missing the past four games with an ankle. He was close to going in Week 9 in Carolina, but the Broncos were cautious with their All-Pro safety.
Meanwhile, all three players who suffered concussions in Carolina returned to practice in full, meaning they've cleared the protocol. Moss and Waddle are starters, so their return will be huge, while Prentice is a key role player who also contributes a lot on special teams.
Don't worry about Allen or Sutton. The Broncos just gave them a vet day of sorts to ease them back into action coming off the bye.
Abrams-Draine and Jones are a little more concerning, being limited, but it's too early to get worried. They've had two weeks to heal up, so we'll monitor Thursday and Friday's practice report, but it would be a surprise if they weren't cleared to play on Sunday.
We're keeping a close eye on tight end Brock Bowers, who suffered a "significant" ankle injury on Sunday against the Seattle Seahawks. He didn't practice on Wednesday, and I wouldn't expect to see that change on Thursday.
If Bowers is a no-go on Friday, he'll likely be ruled out of action. But if he's limited, there's a chance he could play.
People I've talked to close to Raiders HQ aren't sure whether Bowers will play this week, but being the type of competitor he is, it's believed he'll do everything within his power to make it happen.
So, don't sleep on the possibility of Bowers playing in this one. And that's more than a little concerning, given the Broncos' struggles in covering tight ends this season.

title: 5 Broncos Who Have Exceeded Expectations at the Midway Point
full_text:
Even the most optimistic fans would have to admit that the Denver Broncos have exceeded expectations thus far.
Emerging from the bye at 7-2, in a vacuum, isn't all that surprising, especially given that the Broncos won 14 games last season. But with their brutal schedule through the first half of the season, not many many people expected Denver to weather that storm as successfully as it has.
If the Broncos have exceeded expectations as a team, it's because several players have also surprised at the individual level. We've highlighted the Broncos' biggest disappointments , so as promised, it's now time to flip the coin and focus on the five players who've outkicked their coverage coming out of the bye.
I think most Broncos fans believed Coleman was going to be good, but in the four games in which he's actually touched the ball, he's been great. And in each of those games, the rookie fourth-rounder has made his presence felt, contributing to each one of them as a victory.
Since returning from injured reserve in Week 7, Coleman went from the training table to the starting lineup. You don't see that often with a rookie, especially on a Sean Payton team, but since his return, Coleman has outearned J.K. Dobbins in snap and touch share, and it's not even close.
Coleman has carried the ball 47 times for 191 yards (4.1 avg) and three touchdowns, with 13 receptions for 128 yards. His burst and vision have been sorely needed in the Broncos' backfield.
Jonah Coleman gets the @Broncos back in the end zone! DENvsCAR on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/E9pCf15J6A
For a fourth-rounder to be the Broncos' RB1 at the midway point of the season, with $16 million invested in Dobbins and a second-rounder invested in RJ Harvey, it's safe to say that Coleman has exceeded expectations early on. Coleman is a big reason why the Broncos didn't trade for a running back ahead of last week's deadline.
Coleman is really the Broncos' only offensive player I can say has exceeded expectations. It's going to be fun watching the rookie cook down the stretch.
According to John Franklin-Myers , the Broncos didn't even approach him about an extension before he hit free agency and signed with the Tennessee Titans. The Broncos watched his 14.5 sacks walk out the door willingly because they were so confident in Roach.
Roach secured the bag last year during the bye, signing a two-year, $7 million extension . And based on how he's played this season, he's just scratching the surface of his earning potential. The Broncos actually got him at a bargain.
Roach currently ranks third on the team with 25 pressures and has notched four sacks. He's been a force against the run and the pass, and he's showcased a growing penchant for making the clutch-time play.
BRONCOS WIN pic.twitter.com/A4SWB4IO4L
JFM's career-high in sacks came last year with the Broncos, with 7.5. Roach is on pace to surpass it. Heck, Roach could maybe even get to double-digit sacks, as the schedule is opening up for the Broncos post-bye.
Robinson was a 2025 fourth-round pick who spent most of his rookie year as a healthy scratch. But he learned a lot as a rookie, kept developing, and when Jonathon Cooper was placed on the commissioner's exempt list for six weeks to start the season, Robinson capitalized on the opportunity for actual playing time.
Zach Allen leads the pass rush 😤 JAXvsDEN on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/awIGMbyXcq
As a rotational rusher, Robinson is currently tied with Roach for the third-most on the team (25), and he has two sacks. He's been tough for opponents to stop, and a consistent force on the edge.
If things don't go swimmingly for Cooper in his ongoing criminal case, Robinson's Year-2 emergence gives the Broncos plenty of confidence if they have to make a tough decision. No doubt about it, Robinson has been one of the biggest pleasant surprises of the 2026 season.
As the fifth corner on the depth chart, it can be tough to get a snap in edge-wise, but injuries to Patrick Surtain II and Riley Moss vaulted Abrams-Draine onto the field this season. Affectionately known as 'K.A.D.' by the fans, when the chance came to play again on defense, he was more than equal to his opportunity.
K.A.D. notched a crucial interception in the clutch in the Broncos' Week 6 overtime win over the Seatle Seahawks, and he currently ranks third on the team with five pass break-ups. He's also been significantly more reliable as a tackler, with 16 solo tackles thus far.
Kris Abrams-Draine might've made the play of the day for Denver. SEAvsDEN on Prime Video Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/cccQFhEuyP
K.A.D. missed Week 9 with an ankle, but he should be good to go coming out of the bye. I'm excited to see what opportunities may come his way down the stretch for Denver's sticky man in coverage.
It's unsexy, but Crawshaw deserves to be on this list. The 2025 sixth-round pick had an up and down rookie season, but he came on strong down the stretch.
Fast forward to the present moment, and Crawshaw ranks second in the NFL in net punting average (44.2). His coffin-corner punts have helped the Broncos flip field position and pin opponents deep.
As time marches on, the Broncos are looking all the smarter for investing a draft pick in Crawshaw. He could become an All-Pro punter, as soon as this season.

title: Broncos Move Closer to Getting Intriguing Pass-Catching TE Back
full_text:
The Denver Broncos are starting the clock on an intriguing, young — albeit star-crossed — pass-catcher.
9NEWS insider Mike Klis reported Wednesday that Denver has activated tight end Caleb Lohner from injured reserve, opening his 21-day practice window after being sidelined since June with a lower-body injury.
Klis guesses Lohner will likely need to exhaust most of the practice period before a final decision is made on his potential 2026 debut. After 21 days, the team must either place him on the 53-man roster or leave him on injured reserve for the remainder of the season.
A 2025 seventh-round pick , Lohner spent the majority of his rookie campaign on Denver's practice squad, save for a promotion ahead of January's Divisional Round win over the Bills (he was inactive for the game).
Lohner enjoyed an impressive offseason program this past spring, positioning himself as a hidden offensive gem due to his 6-foot-7-inch stature and college basketball background — this, however, was before undergoing a "routine" cleanup procedure on and "setback" with what general manager George Paton later revealed to be his foot.
“He’s looked good. He was having a really good offseason and obviously had a setback with the foot. We expect him, I’m not sure the timetable, mid-season maybe. Don’t hold me to that," Paton told reporters on Aug. 30. "He has all the traits: the size, he can run, he has great ball skills being a basketball player. This would have been a really important preseason and training camp for him. He just needs reps. We’re still excited about him. He’s here every day working, but we won’t see him until late October or so.”
An aforementioned basketball convert, Lohner had a brief but incredibly productive football stint for the Utah Utes, recording 54 receiving yards across four receptions — all of which went for touchdowns. He also scored a two-point conversion.
Upon drafting him, Broncos head coach Sean Payton compared Lohner to his former Pro Bowl tight end with the New Orleans Saints, Jimmy Graham. Payton also singled out the latter in May among the early standouts of the offseason program.
I’ll tell you who stood out, Caleb. He looks entirely different in this camp," Payton said. "Now he was here in this camp a year ago as a draft pick, but he stood out. ... You just start with total reps in the bank in football, and there was just a lot less. You’re drafting traits at that point in the draft. We’ve done that before, and sometimes you’re drafting traits [and] you see a receiving tight end. The one thing I know watching him is he’ll be plenty and very physical."
While it could take Lohner some time to meaningfully see the field — if he does at all — the Broncos' league-worst TE corps offer a fairly easy path to opportunity, with only Evan Engram, Adam Trautman, and Nate Adkins comprising the depth chart.
In a best-case scenario, Lohner will provide quarterback Bo Nix with another big-bodied weapon in the red zone and between the hashes. In a worst-case, he remains buried under the veteran players, his extended absence too much to overcome as far as 2026 is concerned.

title: Courtland Sutton Closing in on Bittersweet Demaryius Thomas Milestone
full_text:
It's been a rough season for Courtland Sutton.
But the Denver Broncos' veteran wide receiver has been an absolute trooper in the face of Jaylen Waddle's rise as the most-targeted pass-catcher, play-calling changes, an early-season Bo Nix slump, and the toughest schedule in the NFL based on opposing defenses.
The Pro Bowler is on pace to post career-low statistics this season, but all that being said, Sutton is poised to join the late, great Demaryius Thomas in the Broncos' all-time record books. By just taking one snap on Sunday against the Las Vegas Raiders , Sutton will tie Thomas for the fifth-most games played by a wide receiver in team history.
It's fitting in so many ways. Thomas is one of the Broncos' two most historically prolific receivers all-time, along with Rod Smith. And it'll likely be a bittersweet moment for Sutton, knowing that Thomas is no longer with us, having passed away suddenly in December 2021.
Thomas was around in 2018 when the Broncos drafted Sutton in the second round to shepherd and show him the ropes. Thomas was later traded to the Houston Texans during Sutton's rookie year, which created a WR1 vacuum in the Broncos' offense.
Although Emmanuel Sanders remained in Denver, for a time, Sutton would be the one to fill that vacuum by season's end. Like Thomas, Sanders would be traded away the following year, which left no doubt about who the Broncos' top gun was at wide receiver.
Sutton dealt with some serious obstacles in Year 2, catching passes from three different starting quarterbacks, including Joe Flacco, Brandon Allen, and a rookie Drew Lock. That only made Sutton's production all the more impressive, finishing with 72 receptions for 1,112 yards and six touchdowns and earning the first Pro Bowl selection of his career.
Fast forward to today, and Sutton is now the second-longest-tenured player on the roster, behind only left tackle Garett Bolles. Sutton has become one of the Broncos' elder statemen, and is looked to for his leadership as a team captain.
At 31, Sutton is still plugging away. Despite the arrival of Waddle, who has outearned him in targets (52 to 46), Sutton remains Nix's security blanket. Sutton stood behind Nix when the going was tough, confident that "the tide" would turn for his quarterback. And it did.
Over the past three weeks, as Nix's confidence and swagger have returned , Sutton's star has risen alongside his quarterback. We're seeing Sutton come down with those contested-catch balls that have been his signature as a pro.
Sutton only has 25 catches for 266 yards and two touchdowns, but he's moved the chains 18 times. The last three games have seen him catch 15 of his 25 balls for 143 yards and a touchdown, so it's clear that something has changed.
Now that the worst of Denver's schedule is in the rear-view, there's every reason to believe that, as Nix continues to build momentum, so will Sutton. When Sunday's game rolls around, it's going to be a cool moment for Sutton to join his former mentor and friend in the Broncos' record books.

title: Grading Every Broncos Position Group at the Midway Point
full_text:
The Denver Broncos are about to emerge from their Week 10 bye.
On Wednesday, the Broncos will begin practicing to host the Las Vegas Raiders this weekend, so this is our last chance to take stock of the team at the midway point of the season — or about as close as is possible to halfway with an odd-numbered 17-game schedule.
We've already posted our individual player grades at the bye and handed out our midseason awards . In our last bye-week deep dive, we're grading each Broncos position group.
Let's get to it and see if we can get a feel for which positions are trending in the right direction for the Broncos' stretch run and which ones need to improve fast.
Bo Nix hasn't been great and for the first six weeks of the season, he was downright bad at times. He was hesitant in his decision-making and jumpy in the pocket, which led to offensive stagnation for long stretches in several games.
However, we must factor in two important things: 1. Nix was recovering from a broken ankle that required two offseason surgeries, and 2. He had to do so while going against the NFL's toughest schedule based on opposing defense .
Because of that, Nix always had the benefit of my doubt. But beginning in Week 7, he no longer needed it, as his confidence came flooding back, and he started looking like the quarterback we saw late last season and in the playoffs before he got hurt.
Despite his protracted slump, Nix still played a winning brand of football. He avoided the negative play — sacks and turnovers — and turned it on in the fourth quarter. Without him, the Broncos aren't anywhere close to 7-2 after the toughest first-half-of-the-season schedule I've ever seen.
Given that Nix's last three games have been so vastly improved, and the fact that he helped to keep Denver winning even while he was still going through a personal storm of sorts, he gets a B- as the only Broncos quarterback to take a snap this season.
The only thing keeping the Broncos' running back grade from a D- or worse has been the emergence of rookie Jonah Coleman. Since he returned from injured reserve in Week 7, the Broncos' rushing offense has improved, but the rookie needs help.
J.K. Dobbins is having a career-worst season, averaging 3.3 yards per carry, while RJ Harvey, before he got hurt, was a relative non-factor as a ball-carrier and not quite as productive as a receiver out of the backfield. Harvey will be eligible to return from IR in Week 13.
This is a position group that could finish the season with a much better grade. But I shudder to think where the Broncos would be without the promise of Coleman.
The Broncos' wide receivers have performed drastically below expectations. But remember: it's a quarterback-dependent position.
Not only were the Broncos' wideouts stuck with Nix's slump and the early-season schematic issues of first-time play-caller Davis Webb, but they also had to go against some of the best secondaries in the NFL. Because of these factors, the benefit of the doubt plays a big part in their midseason grade.
I expected more from Jaylen Waddle, sure. But when Nix has been willing to challenge defenses vertically, he's made great use of Waddle. Now that Nix is hunting again with the football , I expect the second half of the season to be much more prolific for Waddle.
I won't deny that Courtland Sutton has disappointed me this season. He seemed woefully slow early on and unable to separate in coverage. Worst of all, he wasn't fighting for the ball, let alone coming down with it, in contested-catch situations, which has always been his signature play.
Like Nix, though, Sutton has begun to turn it around over the past three weeks, so I'm optimistic that what we saw early on was, again, more a reflection of the level of competition and the quarterback inefficiencies than a true sign that Father Time had taken his toll.
Pat Bryant, when healthy, has been a tremendous boon to the passing offense. Alas, he missed four games with an ankle injury, plus half of the game in which he suffered the injury. But he's back, and immediately made his precence felt by leading the Broncos in receiving yards in Carolina and finding the end zone.
This is another position that could finish with a higher grade than it has at the midway point.
What can I say? The Broncos' top two tight ends can't block, and neither has been able to affect the passing game and create exploitable mismatches.
That's an indictment on Adam Trautman as the Broncos' Y tight end, who is expected to at least be a competent blocker, and Evan Engram , who was signed a year ago to be the 'Joker' weapon that Sean Payton just couldn't wait to plug into this offense.
At this stage, the Broncos are stuck with Engram through the 2026 season, but they'd be wise to give Nate Adkins more of Trautman's reps as the Y tight end, especially if they want to help this run game get off the mat.
I'm not holding my breath, though.
Imagine what this grade might be, were it not for the All-Pro contributions of left tackle Garett Bolles and right guard Quinn Meinerz holding things together. Even their impact hasn't been enough to keep center Luke Wattenberg and right tackle Mike McGlinchey from turning in bottom-of-the-league bodies of work at their respective positions.
Left guard Ben Powers has been solid, though he unfairly catches some lashings from fans that should be directed at Wattenberg. Powers has been the least of the Broncos' primary O-line culprits.
Garett Bolles simply REFUSES to give up sacks https://t.co/DZjMOmP80c pic.twitter.com/NmM1LSR8cW
The good news is that McGlinchey has begun to play much better over the past few weeks, so I'm hopeful that the bye, combined with the Broncos not having to face an elite opponent on a weekly basis, can lead to Wattenberg improving, too. Again, the run blocking hasn't been good, but the Broncos' O-line stays in the green grade-wise, thanks not only to Bolles and Meinerz, but also because they've allowed the fewest sacks in the NFL.
It could and must be so much better, though.
Zach Allen is once again delivering All-Pro results, with the most QB pressures on the team and co-leading in sacks, with 4.5. He's also one of the NFL's most stout interior run defenders; he's as good as it gets.
D.J. Jones has been hit-and-miss, while Eyioma Uwazurike failed to launch as the Broncos' succession plan for John Franklin-Myers, or at least half of it. Malcolm Roach, though? He represents the other half of the Broncos' post-JFM plan, and he's been more than equal to his opportunity.
With Uwazurike on IR for the next few weeks, the Broncos will have to rely more on Sai'vion Jones, Jordan Jackson, and rookie third-rounder Tyler Onyedim. Hopefully, we see Onyedim continue to dress and get more snaps, because he can actually help turn around the Broncos' woes against the run, as he flashed in Week 9's win over the Carolina Panthers in his first-ever game.
Allen and Roach make this grade. D.J. Jones does well as an interior pass rusher on a part-time basis, but he's been straight mugged in the run game. It's been nice to see Sai'vion Jones get more playing time, but the Broncos' best hope of elevating this D-line may be getting Onyedim on the field more.
Nik Bonitto struggled to get home over the first few weeks of the season, but it wasn't for a lack of trying. He still impacted the game with consistent pressure, and at the halfway point, shares the team sack lead with Allen (4.5).
Jonathon Cooper's return came at an opportune time. Que Robinson continues to do a great job as a depth rusher, but Jonah Elliss did not seem ready to start opposite Bonitto for the first six weeks while Cooper was on the commissioner's exempt list, and then he suffered a lower-leg injury in Week 6 that landed him on IR.
Robinson has been one of the Broncos' biggest pleasant surprises of the season. With Cooper back in the starting lineup, the Broncos' edge presence again looks like we've come to expect over the past few…

title: This Jaw-Dropping Bo Nix Stat Changes the Conversation
full_text:
Say what you will about Bo Nix, but he's a winner.
Despite all the shade Nix gets, nobody can take that away from the Denver Broncos' quarterback, especially after he led his team to a 7-2 start in the face of a gauntlet of tier-one defenses and top-gun quarterbacks in the first half of the season.
Nix's winning ways are nothing new. He delivered 10 wins as a rookie in 2024, snapping the Broncos' previous eight-year playoff drought.
In Year 2, Nix tied the Broncos' single-season record of 14 wins, dethroned Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs as AFC West champions, and secured the AFC's No. 1 playoff seed. Alas, that magical 2025 campaign came to a crashing halt when Nix suffered a broken ankle on the third-to-last play of Broncos' 33-30 overtime win over the Buffalo Bills in the divisional round.
Every Broncos fan can remember where he or she was when the Nix injury news broke. It was devestating.
Bouncing back from that ankle injury, which required two offseason surgeries, was arduous for Nix. His physical injury seemed to heal a bit faster than his psychological wounds, as his early-season struggles seemed to illustrate, but he still found ways to win against some of the NFL's best teams.
According to Gridiron Stats & Info , Nix and the Broncos have faced "the hardest schedule of opposing defenses" so far this season. That's why Nix and Denver's offense deserve the benefit of the doubt, and why optimism should reign supreme as the schedule opens up.
Despite that tough row to hoe, Nix finds himself among elite company in terms of winning percentage halfway through his third season. As Pro Football Focus illustrated in the graphic below, Nix currently ranks sixth all-time in winning percentage through a quarterback's first three seasons since the NFL merger (1966).
Fast starters pic.twitter.com/5rgYdrLWaP
Only Lamar Jackson (.811), Dan Marino (.805), Patrick Mahomes (.774), Russell Wilson (.750), and Ben Roethlisberger (.725) had a better winning percentage thorugh their first three seasons than Nix currently does. And with the Broncos' schedule opening up dramatically after the bye, Nix will have the chance to climb well into the top-five in this statistical area.
Nix wasn't quite himself to start the 2026 season, which was as concerning as it was disappointing . Despite his assurances that he was healthy, something between the ears seemed off, but his confidence and swagger returned with gusto after he rushed for a 62-yard touchdown against the Arizona Cardinals in Week 7.
BO NIX 62-YARD TOUCHDOWN RUN DENvsAZ on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/sxC4uWF33r
Counting that game, Nix has exceeded the 200-yard passing mark in the three games leading into the bye. He's built up a nice head of steam for the stretch run.
The hesitancy and jumpiness in the pocket we saw from Nix over the first six games are gone, and he's playing with so much more confidence. The most exciting development? He's hunting with the football again , which will pay dividends coming out of the bye with Jaylen Waddle returning from a concussion.
Amid his early-season slump, as some Broncos fans and local media pundits began calling for Nix to be benched, he shrugged off the criticism and talked about his goal of "peaking" at the right time, which he just reemphasized on the Manning Cast — joining Peyton and Eli Manning — during Monday Night Football .
"I feel good about the spot we're in. Obviously, we've had a tough schedule thus far. We've played some really good teams, but we feel like there's a lot more out there for us that we can accomplish," Nix said on the Manning Cast .
"We don't feel like we're playing our best in certain spots, but it's a long season, and in my opinion, you definitely don't want to peak at the beginning. You want to be peaking as you're going into the playoffs, so we're 7-2, and we're in a good spot."
Bo Nix on the #ManningCast tonight talking to Peyton and Eli about how he feels about the #Broncos coming out of the bye week. And breaking a record held by Peyton. #BroncosCountry @DenverChannel pic.twitter.com/6L8dhJv7rV
The "Star Wars" numbers haven't necessarily been there for Nix, in terms of individual stats, and yet, he became the only quarterback in NFL history to pass for 7,500-plus yards and 50-plus touchdowns while winning 20-plus games in his first two seasons. So it's not as if he's turned in Tebow-esque statistical numbers.
Nix has already set many franchise and NFL records. His first three years have been unprecedented in Broncos history, and while it's a shame he suffered that ill-timed ankle injury on the doorstep of the Super Bowl, his hard work to get back for this season has already paid off.
The Broncos are in a great situation coming out of the bye. It feels like Denver is on a collision course with the Bills to decide the No. 1 seed, which could be decided when the two teams throw down on Christmas Day (Week 16) at Mile High.
The Broncos' bye came at a beneficial juncture this season. The NFL may have brutally frontloaded their schedule, but at least the Broncos' bye came at as close to the midway point of the season as it gets.
It's going to be fun watching Nix continue to stack wins down the stretch, as he looks to climb well into the top-five quarterbacks in winning percentage over his first three NFL seasons.

title: Sean Payton Cracks Door for Broncos ILB Red Murdock to See Field
full_text:
Speaking for the first time since the Denver Broncos completed their bye week, Denver Broncos head coach Sean Payton addressed the failed trade for Chargers linebacker Daiyan Henley that occurred during that period .
While insisting that no " loophole " had been invoked to veto the deal, Payton generally kept a casual tone toward Henley, whom the Broncos admittedly still covet.
“Nothing changed. It was already stated," Payton told reporters via conference call on Monday. "Everything was pretty clearly spelled out. I’m not going to get into the specifics. He’s a prospect we thought—and still do [think]—very highly of. It just didn’t work out and it’s not uncommon with trades. That’s kind of where it went, and I’ll leave it at that.”
More interestingly, Payton was asked for his thoughts on the state of Denver's current inside linebacker corps, which would've been shaken up had the team acquired Henley.
“I don’t view it the same way you do," he said. "We’re going to play the starters and then guys that earn reps certainly will earn playing time. Yes, that’s all I could say to that.”
The Broncos' botched acquisition of Henley was, intentionally or not, an admission that they aren't perfectly satisfied with Alex Singleton and Justin Strnad as the starting ILBs. Henley was specifically targeted — from a division rival, no less — and Denver wanted him badly enough to give up two draft picks.
They can claim he was supposed to be "depth," but the Broncos likely had long-term plans for a 27-year-old who wears the green dot in Los Angeles, is an excellent blitzer, and is solid in coverage. (And who's scheduled to become a free agent in 2027.)
With Henley now out of the picture, there's theoretically a chance the team could promote intriguing seventh-round rookie Red Murdock from the practice squad — perhaps not in the days ahead, but by the end of the season.
Murdock had a strong preseason and, as the NCAA's all-time leader in career forced fumbles, would bring a different element to an already elite defensive unit.
“It’s pretty up there," he said in August regarding his confidence level. "I’m very confident I can play at this level, but also confident in the little margins that I need to improve on [because] it can make a big difference when playing at a high level.”
One way or the other, whether it's with Murdock, Karene Reid, or Jordan Turner, the Broncos must begin preparing for their long-term future at the position, which almost certainly won't include Singleton or Strnad. If somebody can be that guy, they need to find out sooner rather than later.

title: Broncos' 7-2 Start Has Overshadowed These Five Disappointments
full_text:
The Denver Broncos are 7-2 coming out of the bye, which means there's way more positive to focus on than negative.
But it hasn't all been pretty. It's tough to be too hard on the Broncos, though, given how brutal the first half of their schedule truly was.
The Broncos faced the Kansas City Chiefs twice, all four teams of the NFC West, plus the Jacksonville Jaguars, so a little benefit of the doubt is warranted. But as we take stock of this team entering its stretch run , I'm breaking down the Broncos' biggest disappointments of 2026.
Don't worry; there will be a biggest pleasant surprises edition, too. With that said, let's dive in.
Everyone was excited for Sean Payton's wunderkind to get his chance to call the plays. The hope was that Webb's close relationship with Bo Nix, combined with his talent for offense and coaching, which were heard about often from Payton himself, would lead to big things for the Broncos.
Alas, it didn't. The Broncos were a mostly out-of-sync offense through the first quarter of the season, and Nix looked like a quarterback who'd regressed alarmingly in Year 3. The Broncos weathered the storm at 2-2, but both of their wins were of the comeback variety.
That hasn't changed since Payton took back the play-calling , by the way. Six of Denver's seven wins have been by a single-score margin. But since Payton began calling the plays again in Week 5, Nix and the offense have steadily improved.
I'll always wonder how it may have shaken out for Webb as the play-caller if the NFL had structured the Broncos' schedule a bit more evenly this season, instead of frontloading it with a gauntlet of opponents with top-tier defenses. Webb has taken his demotion of sorts in stride, but in the wake of his meteoric rise through the coaching ranks since 2023, it was the first setback of his young career.
I wish it were otherwise, but Dobbins has been a colossal disappointment this year. Part of the reason for that is the fresh memory of how good he looked in the 10 games he played for the Broncos last year, rushing for 772 yards, but he's looked like a shell of that player.
Dobbins still leads the Broncos in rushing (324 yards), but his 3.3 yards-per-carry average is a career-low. He still has time to improve his rushing efficiency, but he'll be doing so as the No. 2 running back behind Jonah Coleman.
The Broncos re-signed Dobbins to a two-year, $16 million extension in the spring, which amounted to a 4x raise, and that's another reason why the disappointment surrounding his season thus far has been so sharp. The Broncos sniffed around the running back trade block ahead of last week's deadline, and ultimately didn't make a move, but Dobbins's name was reportedly floated in some of those talks.
Since Coleman returned from injured reserve in Week 7, Dobbins has been relegated to a supporting role, and it's not even close. Payton maintains that Dobbins is still "a big part" of what the Broncos are doing offensively down the stretch, but after nine games of relative impotence, I'll believe it when I see it.
Denver's All-Pro tandem of left tackle Garett Bolles and right guard Quinn Meinerz get a pass, because they've been excellent this season, but the other three starters have been a disappointment. There's no way around it.
Center Luke Wattenberg and right tackle Mike McGlinchey have been two of the NFL's worst players at their respective positions, and it's been reflected in the Broncos' run-game inefficiency. Pass protection-wise, they've been a little bit better, but these two are a big reason for the run game's failure to launch.
So, in that sense, it's not all on Dobbins, but Coleman has been able to still make hay behind this O-line, and create for himself, thanks to his burst and vision. The O-line could do so much more to help Coleman and Dobbins coming out of the bye, and we know that Payton and company have been hyper-focued on improving it.
Time will tell, but don't blame left guard Ben Powers . He hasn't exactly played at a Pro Bowl level, but he's the least of the Broncos' O-line culprits this season.
Man, Engram's season started off on the right foot, scoring the Broncos' only touchdown in their Week 1 loss to the Chiefs. But it's pretty much been all downhill for the veteran tight end since then.
Engram has 17 catches for 169 yards and one touchdown through nine games. He's been asked to block a lot more than he did last year, as the Broncos have moved to more two-tight-end sets, but it hasn't translated to more targets or production.
This is the last year of Engram's deal. He's on the wrong side of 30, and has failed to live up to expectations. He'll likely hit the bricks in the offseason, but the Broncos have to find a way to get younger and better at tight end in 2027 because that position's inefficiencies have also played a big role in their rushing struggles.
Nix makes this list, but he was also my selection for team MVP at the midway point of the season . He remains the Broncos' most valuable player, though that doesn't mean he's their best player.
Without Nix and his clutch-time excellence, the Broncos don't weather the storm of that initial gauntlet at 7-2. We'd be talking about a 2-7 team, maybe a 3-6 squad, if Jarrett Stidham had been the quarterback against defenses like Kansas City (twice), the Rams, the Jaguars, the 49ers, and even the Chargers.
That being said, it wouldn't be a fair list of disappointments if Nix wasn't mentioned. His first six games of the season were concerning. He was indecisive, hesitant, and jumpy in the pocket.
Bo's ankle may have been 100%, but his psyche, in returning from that injury, hadn't quite caught up to the physical recovery. His confidence needed a big boost, and that was honestly a big reason why Payton made the fateful decision to take back the play-calling from Webb: he needed to get Nix back on track, and salvage his self-confidence before it was possibly too late.
Nix's confidence and swagger came flooding back in Week 7 when he rushed for a 62-yard touchdown on that surgically-repaired ankle, and he hasn't looked back. The Broncos are still questing for a full four-quarters version of Nix, but his comportment over the past three games isn't even comparable to his first six games.
I've consistently maintained that the Broncos will go as far as Nix can take them, and even amid his early-season slump, he was still able to do enough to beat some damn good teams and outduel some top-tier quarterbacks, including Patrick Mahomes, Trevor Lawrence, Matthew Stafford, and Justin Herbert, the last of whom makes this short list because Nix had never beaten him before until Week 5.
The Broncos could still get out to a 7-2 start without Nix playing his best ball along the way. Now imagine the heights this team could reach with him firing on all cylinders.
Nix is on the rise, and his goal of peaking at the right time — down the stretch and into the playoffs — is very much on the table. He's back; of that, I have no doubt. But I couldn't go through this article without mentioning how disappointing his first few games of this season truly were.

title: New Mock Draft Predicts Broncos Will Fix What Trade Deadline Couldn't
full_text:
The Denver Broncos had linebacker on the brain ahead of last week's NFL trade deadline.
Given the missed tackles and coverage miscues of Alex Singleton and Justin Strnad, the Broncos agreed to a trade for Los Angeles Chargers linebacker Daiyan Henley, but the deal fell through when he failed his physical. Henley would have brought tackling reliability and coverage chops to the middle of the Broncos' defense.
Still unsigned by the Chargers, there's a chance Henley will hit free agency in March, at which point, the Broncos could try to pursue him with a compensation package more in line with their concerns about the arthritis in his knee. But if that doesn't happen, for one reason or another, Denver could be resolved to look to the draft for a linebacker.
NFL Draft On SI 's Justin Melo has mostly been mocking tight ends to the Broncos in Round 1. Last week, he mocked an offensive tackle — which could well be in the cards this time around — but in his latest post-trade-deadline iteration, Melo had the Broncos taking Notre Dame linebacker Kyngstonn Viliamu-Asa at No. 24 overall.
"Denver Broncos linebacker Alex Singleton turns 33 in December. It will be among the positions that require an investment this offseason. Notre Dame linebacker Kyngstonn Viliamu-Asa has been a riser. He's an athletic specimen with more upside to explore," Melo wrote .
Age is definitely a factor for Denver at linebacker. Both Singleton and Strnad are on the wrong side of 30, even if both are under contract through the 2027 season.
Viliamu-Asa would offer the Broncos great run-defending upside and also some coverage chops. He would need to develop both aspects of his game further to really thrive in the NFL, but the tools are there.
Listed at 6-foot-3 and 234 pounds, Viliamu-Asa has the prototypical size NFL teams like at linebacker, which was one of the potential drawbacks with Henley, who checks in at 6-foot-0 and 225 pounds. Viliamu-Asa can get off blocks and has the size and strength to mix it up in the box.
It's been a long time since the Broncos drafted an inside linebacker in the first round. The last linebacker to hear his name called by Denver in Round 1 was D.J. Williams back in 2004 during the late-era Mike Shanahan regime.
Since then, the highest the Broncos have drafted an inside linebacker is in Round 3, with Nate Irving in 2011 and Drew Sanders in 2023. Neither linebacker panned out well, though Irving at least played out his rookie deal in Denver.
The Broncos drafted Red Murdock with the last pick of the 2026 draft, but he didn't make the 53-man roster. He has stuck around on the practice squad, though, developing under the watchful eye of this coaching staff, so he'll live to fight another day, and maybe make a push in 2027.
But Denver can't bank on that happening. Singleton and Strnad have displayed their limitations, and with how talented the Broncos are up front and in the secondary, they've been able to get away with it at he second level of the defense.
However, it's high time the Broncos invested some premium resources in an inside linebacker. I'm not 100% sure Viliamu-Asa is the right fit for Denver, and time will tell whether he lives up to Melo's first-round projections, but drafting him would certainly signal a recognition on the team's part that it needs to improve dramatically at linebacker after this season.

title: Lions Draw Official With Past Controversial Call For Buccaneers Game
full_text:
The officiating crew for the Detroit Lions ' Week 11 game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers has been revealed.
When the Lions return to Ford Field on Sunday, their game against Tampa Bay will be officiated by Adrian Hill and his crew. Hill has been a lead referee since the 2019 season, and has  officiated nine Lions games in his career with Detroit holding a 3-6 record in those games.
Hill did not ref a Lions game last year, with his most recent assignment for Detroit coming in the 2024 season when he presided over their shootout loss to the Buffalo Bills at Ford Field.
It has been a bit of an up-and-down year for Hill. He drew the assignment for the first game of the NFL season in Seattle between the Seahawks and Patriots,  but also served a one-game suspension for an incident during his Week 5 assignment.
In that game, which was between the Minnesota Vikings and Miami Dolphins, Hill was knocked to the ground inadvertandly by Vikings linebacker Eric Wilson, who was blocked into the ref by Dolphins running back Ollie Gordon.
After the collision, Hill appeared to get up angrily and had choice words for Wilson. The NFL reviewed the incident and elected to suspend him one game for unprofessional conduct.
Hill also has some history with the Lions . He officiated Detroit's 37-35 loss to the Minnesota Vikings that would be the final game of the Matt Stafford era and end the 2020 season.
In that game, the Lions appeared to have a stop when Tracy Walker had a sack of Kirk Cousins on a fourth-down early in the fourth quarter, but Walker was called for a controversial roughing the passer penalty. The penalty extended the drive and led to a Vikings touchdown.
Sunday's game between the Lions and Buccaneers won't be the first time Hill has presided over a game between these two teams. He was the head ref when these squads met at Ford Field in 2019, with the Tom Brady-led Buccaneers winning 38-17.
Hill's crew ranks fifth in the league in flags per game with 16, and his total of nine penalties dismissed is the least amongst any crew that has officiated more than two games. He is coming off reffing the Monday Night Football game between the Ravens and Chargers, which featured a season-low in flags for his crew with 10.
The most common flags thrown by his crew are false start and offensive holding, as there have been 30 and 23 total flags in those categories by his crew.

title: 4 Key Detroit Lions Facing Most Pressure With Aidan Hutchinson Out
full_text:
The Detroit Lions have a big absence to account for on the defensive line for the remainder of the 2026 season.
Aidan Hutchinson suffered a torn ACL, meaning he will miss the rest of the year. He won't be easy to replace, and becomes the latest Lion to suffer a significant injury. As a result, the Lions' defense has several players who will need to step up moving forward.
Here are the four players facing the most pressure after Hutchinson was lost for the season.
The rookie defensive end has taken a big step forward as of late. It was a quiet start to the year, as he went the first four games of the season playing less than 20 snaps. However, an injury to DJ Wonnum gave him an opportunity in Week 9, and then Hutchinson's injury did the same in Week 10.
In each of those games, Moore recorded two sacks. This indicates the potential he has as a player, but now the expectations will be ratcheted up for him. The recent hot streak has been an intriguing development, but with Hutchinson out Moore has to be a consistent producer opposite of Wonnum.
Through nine games, McNeill is playing at an All-Pro level. The interior lineman has 6.5 sacks, which is a phenomenal number for a player who plays his position. Having McNeill producing at that level from the interior line has been a huge asset for the Lions, as he's exploited some of the extra attention being paid to Hutchinson by winning his 1-on-1 matchups.
However, with Hutchinson out it could be McNeill that sees the extra attention moving forward. While it's been a great bounce-back season for him, opposing teams are more aware of the impact he has on the game by this point in the season.
McNeill will likely see more double teams at the point of attack in pass-rush situations moving forward, and will need to continue playing at a high level even if that doesn't result in more sacks.
A first-round pick of the Lions last year, Williams has yet to make himself a household name as a pass-rusher. Williams has been solid against the run, but hasn't been a difference maker in passing downs. Without Hutchinson, that could change.
Williams was billed as being a player who is growing in that area, but he hasn't been asked to play much as a pass-rusher with the emergence of rookie Skyler Gill-Howard.
If the Lions want to get bigger on the defensive line without Hutchinson, though, it could involve using McNeill as a 5-tech or potentially a big end and keeping Williams on the field with Gill-Howard.
Wonnum is the veteran of the room, and his role just got magnified with Hutchinson out. Never considered to be a rush-first defensive end, he has been quite productive for Detroit to the tune of six sacks through his first eight games.
Now, Wonnum is two off a career-high and will have plenty of chances to get there. He's been the edge-setting force for the defense opposite of Hutchinson, and has done a fine job of handling that up to this point.
However, with Hutchinson no longer in the mix, teams may be less inclined to run at him as they try to expose the other side of the defense. Wonnum will need to be consistent moving forward to help stabilize a defense that is without one of its biggest leaders.

title: Dan Campbell Turns Heads With Recent Comments About DE Ahmed Hassanein
full_text:
The Detroit Lions feel they have enough depth to navigate the injury to star defensive end Aidan Hutchinson.
On Wednesday afternoon, head coach Dan Campbell expressed that he wanted to get second-year defensive end Ahmed Hassanein going a "little bit" against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.
For the first nine games of the 2026 NFL regular season, the former sixth-round draft pick has been inactive, causing many to wonder why he was not seeing much playing time, especially since he had a solid training camp in the summer.
The former NFL tight end expressed earlier this week he feels the roster is better equipped to handle the loss of Hutchinson than back in 2024, when the former first-round pick was lost for the season, after a severe leg injury suffered against the Dallas Cowboys.
“Yeah, we are much better equipped than we were then," said Campbell. "That's the reason why we have the depth that we have in that room. We knew that was important. I mean, these are the things that you learn over a six-year period, is how important depth is. And so, we feel really good about that room. Now I mentioned this before, (Alim McNeill) Mac is playing at a high level. He's got to continue to do that and then some. (DJ) Wonnum, it was good to get him back. He's got to continue to play at a high level and we need even a little bit more. Derrick Moore, hey, he looks good, he's improving. We need more."
Detroit has also been stout along the interior of the defensive line, led by McNeill, Gill-Howard and Tyleik Williams.
"Gill-Howard, we need more. Tyleik (Williams), we need more. We can keep going here a little bit, but the good news is those guys are improving, they're getting better and they're playing as one unit. And so, got a ton of faith in those guys," said Campbell. "And so yeah, we'll be able to handle this. And our backend's playing pretty good right now.
"Our backers are doing a good job. And really, we're using the totality of that roster, that defensive roster. (Defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard) Shepp's doing a good job, those coaches, and really all of them have a role and a hand in this. And that's probably, you say, 'What's the strength of our defense right now?' They're playing as one unit.”

title: Jahmyr Gibbs Earns NFC Offensive Player of Week After Patriots Win
full_text:
Detroit Lions running back Jahmyr Gibbs has been recognized again by the National Foorbtal League for his stellar efforts against the New England Patriots in Germany.
After securing 153 rushing yards on 22 carries, two touchdowns and seven receptions for 99 yards, (252 all-purpose yards) the former first-round draft pick was named the NFC Offensive Player of the Week.
Detroit Lions quarterback Jared Goff commented postgame about Gibbs' monster performance in a
“I think we got to pinch ourselves sometimes and not take it for granted how special he is. He’s just so explosive with the ball in his hands. We threw that check down to him; it goes 50 yards. That’s so rare for a guy to be able to do all the things he does," said Goff. "Now he’s becoming this back that can protect as well. It’s a complete back. He’s as good as anyone in the league. I love playing with him.”
Among the biggest reasons the Lions' rushing attack has been potent has been the willingness of receivers and tight ends to block for Gibbs.
Second-year wideout Isaac TeSlaa was rewarded for his blocking efforts with a receiving touchdown against New England.
Additional Detroit Lions NFL Insider Analysis: 2026 Midseason Offensive Grades
“I don't think I could express enough the appreciation for that. I've pointed out numerous times to him, to the offense. It's a huge part of who we are," said offensive coordinator Drew Petzing. "Ultimately, it's who he is, which makes him - like yes, he's not showing up on the stat sheet every week, but he has an immense impact on the game and how we do things as an offense. And I think he knows that. I hope he knows that. I've made that very clear to him, I think, because it is. It's a big part of who we are and it's not an easy thing to do and he takes a ton of pride in it."

title: Detroit Lions Are Touchdown Favorites Against Buccaneers in Week 11
full_text:
The Detroit Lions (7-2) will look to capture their sixth straight victory when they take on the likely Baker Mayfield-less Buccaneers (3-6) Sunday.
The Lions are coming off a 35-10 beatdown of the New England Patriots in Munich, Germany. Meanwhile, Tampa Bay, which has won two of its last three games, had its bye in Week 10.
Per DraftKings, the Lions, without defensive captains Jack Campbell and Aidan Hutchinson, are presently seven-point favorites to beat the Buccaneers in the Week 11 tilt.
The Buccaneers last played in Week 9 on Sunday Night Football against the Bears, suffering a 27-24 loss to Ben Johnson's team. Mayfield did start the game, and proceeded to throw two interceptions and complete just 56.3 percent of his passes.
The ninth-year passer has had a rough season in Tampa Bay. In six games, he's thrown for more interceptions (four) than touchdowns (three), and has completed only 60.6 percent of his passes. Additionally, his QBR of 32.0 ranks 29th among 31 qualified signal-callers.
Mayfield's backup, rookie Jalon Daniels, hasn't fared much better. Daniels has suited up for five games and made three starts, and has completed 61.2 percent of his passes while throwing for three touchdowns and five interceptions.
Altogether, the Buccaneers have struggled to do much of anything through the air. In fact, they've amassed the least amount of passing yards (1,277) and passing touchdowns (six) through the season's first 10 weeks.
To add insult to injury, Mayfield’s status for Sunday is uncertain as the result of a foot strain. Subsequently, it'll be very interesting to see the type of injury designation Tampa Bay tags him with on its injury report Wednesday.
Meanwhile, on defense, the Buccaneers have been much more productive. They've not only allowed the sixth-fewest points per game (19.8), but they've also been extremely stout against the run. In fact, the Todd Bowles-led squad has allowed both the fewest rushing yards (712) and the fewest touchdowns on the ground (three) so far this season. It's a testament to the fact that Tampa Bay is a better team than its record indicates.
Lions head man Dan Campbell shares the sentiment and expects a dogfight with the Buccaneers Sunday.
“This will be a big one. It's a physical team. These guys play with violence,” Campbell told reporters Tuesday. “(Buccaneers head coach) Todd Bowles has always done a great job. The record is not indicative of the type of team that they are. They're in the hunt for the South. And so, we know what we have in front of us, but no excuses. We're back from Germany. We know this is number two here in this little stretch we've got, and our guys will be ready to play.”
The Lions and the Buccaneers are set to kick off from Ford Field on Sunday at 1 p.m. (EST).

title: Detroit Lions 2026 Midseason Grades: Offense
full_text:
The Detroit Lions are off to a solid start, finishing the first half of their season with a 7-2 record.
While they still have work to do over the season's final two months, Detroit has the ability to be serious contenders for a third NFC North crown in four years. They will enter Week 11 with the No. 2 seed in the NFC playoffs, and have an opportunity to continue helping themselves against NFC opponents.
The Lions have been fueled by a number of solid performances on the offensive side of the ball. They currently have multiple players who could be realistic awards candidates should they continue to play at a high level.
Here are grades for each Lions offensive position group as the season passes its midway point.
For the better part of the first half, Jared Goff was playing at an elite level with no turnovers through the first five games. However, things have turned a bit sour as he has turned the ball over four times over the team's last three games.
Though this recent stretch of turnovers has put a damper on his performance, he has still been one of the most consistent passers in the league throughout the first half. He's fifth in the league in passing yards per game, and has largely been efficient during the team's 7-2 start.
While Goff has had his flaws with mobility exposed at times, the Lions have been able to rely on him throughout the season with how consistent he's been. He remains one of the most effective pre-snap quarterbacks in the league, which allowed him to have success against defenses like Minnesota's earlier in the year.
Jahmyr Gibbs is making a serious case to be named Offensive Player of the Year with his phenomenal start to the season. Gibbs has shown himself to be one of the most dynamic players of the league, with four games of over 150 rushing yards within the team's first nine.
Gibbs has undoubtedly asserted himself amongst the league's top running backs, and continues to make strides in other facets of his game as well. The running back is growing as a pass-protector, and has been utilized heavily in the passing game at times as well.
With Isiah Pacheco missing the entire season up to this point, the Lions have leaned on Sione Vaki as the backup to Gibbs. It's proven to be a good fit, as Vaki runs tough and has some pop as a ball-carrier as he's shown.
Like Gibbs, Vaki is also making improvements in the pass-protection element of the game. It remains to be seen whether Gibbs' hefty workload is sustainable, but he's on pace for a stellar season with the way he's started the year.
The Lions have gotten plenty of production out of wideout Amon-Ra St. Brown , who appears to be trending toward another 1,000-yard season in his fifth NFL campaign. He has proven to be one of the league's most durable players, and this year has been no different.
St. Brown is tied-for-third with seven receiving touchdowns, while he ranks ninth in receiving yards at 755.
Jameson Williams has not had the level of consistent production that has been to be expected from him after back-to-back 1,000-yard seasons, but he has still proven to be a big play threat at times. His explosive play rate is down, but he appears to be more well-rounded as a receiver and has delivered big moments such as the game-winner against Minnesota.
Elsewhere, Isaac TeSlaa hasn't had the breakout season many believed he would but has still delivered in some key situations, such as fourth-downs and his first touchdown of the season in the red-zone last week.
The Lions and Sam LaPorta have had some back-and-forth and appear to have reached a standstill in terms of a future contract extension. With all this going on, the Lions have utilized LaPorta less in recent weeks, coincedence or not.
LaPorta is ultimately a huge part of the Lions' offensive attack, as his presence alone is another weapon other teams would have to account for on Detroit's roster. It wouldn't be easy at all for Detroit to replace him, which is why I think a deal ultimately gets done.
Still, LaPorta hasn't had an elite season at this point in the year, and could be utilized more in the coming weeks. Brock Wright has been reliable as a run-blocker, while Tyler Conklin has usurped the youngster Jackson Meeks for the third tight end spot.
The Lions' offensive line has been maligned at times for all the changes they've undergone. Taylor Decker is gone, while Penei Sewell has switched over to the left side to account for that loss. As a result, the team is playing two necomers in center Juice Scruggs and right tackle first-round pick Blake Miller.
Scruggs has been thrust into action, and made the most of it by how well he's playing. Added via the David Montgomery trade last year, Scruggs was forced into playing center after an injury to Cade Mays who has made just two starts this season.
Scruggs and Miller have been solid additions, while Christian Mahogany and Tate Ratledge have both taken their abilities up a notch at the guard position. Moving forward, the Lions have positioned themselves to have one of the best young offensive lines across the board, as they have been solid particularly in the run game paving the way for Gibbs.
