title: Packers Report Card: Grades From Another Beatdown Against Vikings
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – The grades are in and, as you’d suspect, they resemble my marks in high school geometry. OK, jokes aside, even I was not as bad as the Packers were in Sunday’s game against the Minnesota Vikings.
In what was billed as a showdown between two of the top teams in the NFC, the Vikings dismantled the Packers in every perceivable fashion.
Arguably the best play of the game for Green Bay’s offense was one that probably should never have happened. Jordan Love threw a ball down the middle of the field for Tucker Kraft in the third quarter that bounced off his hands, off a defender’s hands, and into the arms of Savion Williams. The play was good for 25 yards, and could only be chalked up to sheer dumb luck.
That’s basically all the Packers had on Sunday. Here are our grades from a dreadful performance.
The success of this game was going to be on the shoulders of Green Bay’s offensive line. If the Packers could protect Jordan Love, the offense would have an opportunity against Minnesota’s secondary to put up some points.
If they couldn’t, it was going to be a long day for the offense. The score was 20-0 in favor of the Vikings in the middle of the third quarter. Jordan Love was sacked eight times in the first two-and-a-half quarters as the Vikings built an insurmountable lead.
When Love was pressured, he was snowed under. When he wasn’t, it was almost as if he was anticipating pressure. He sailed the ball over Tucker Kraft’s head on an interception that came as he was fading away from the throw. Even if Kraft is at fault for cutting off his route, Love’s process was bad on the play.
Love was actually better under pressure (11-of-14) than from a clean pocket (6-of-13 with his one touchdown and one interception). It’s just that the frequency of the pressure – 62.9 percent, according to Pro Football Focus – either led to sacks or simply made him uneasy on most dropbacks.
The Vikings defense pressured Jordan Love on 21 of 35 dropbacks (60.0%) and sacked him 8 times. Love faced a career-high pressure rate despite averaging 2.33 seconds to throw, his second-quickest time in a game. @MINvsGB | #Skol
“I think to your point, you take some hits in the game, things like that. As a quarterback, that’s the job,” Love said of the interception, when he acted as if pressure was coming when he actually had a strong pocket.
“You’ve got to be able to stay in there and trust the guys are going to get the job done around you and still be able to deliver. So, I’ll never make an excuse for that. You’ve got to be able to sit in the pocket and just trust what’s going on around you. And we didn’t do that on that play.”
Tyrod Taylor entered the game because of the lopsided nature of the score.
Love and Co. had very few answers for Brian Flores. They showed little interest in a quick passing game that likely needs to be employed against a defense like Minnesota’s. Instead, they tried their bombs-away offense but never had time to find any shots down the field.
They did find a little success in the second half when they switched to a no-huddle offense, but it was too late by then.
Christian Watson and Matthew Golden, who caught 17-of-18 targets for 335 yards last week, caught 8-of-13 for 107 yards vs. Minnesota. PFF charged Golden with two drops. Kraft had one catch for a second consecutive week.
Green Bay’s offense goes by Jordan Love and their passing game. They went nowhere on Sunday.
Perhaps the Packers have found something with Kaleb Johnson leading the way in their backfield? Green Bay’s bar to clear in the run game is incredibly low, but Johnson looked decisive on his runs and was averaging 4.2 yards per carry before the game got out of hand.
Of course, part of the reason the game got out of hand was the Packers’ need to be one-dimensional because of the scoreboard and their inability to consistently rely on their run game.
Josh Jacobs will likely take his role as starting running back when he returns from his finger injury, perhaps as soon as next week against the Rams or perhaps the following week. In the meantime, Johnson needs to be the one who is the bell cow, if such a thing exists for the 2026 Packers.
The good was that the Packers sacked Kirk Cousins three times and picked him off once. They held him to 207 yards on 21 completions. The bad? They gave up three huge third-down conversions that were at least 12 yards in length.
One was a 38-yard touchdown to Myles Price to give the Vikings a 10-0 lead in the first quarter.
The final one was a third-and-12 in which Minnesota was set up in a formation that made a receiver screen feel inevitable. Cousins got the ball to Justin Jefferson quickly and Jefferson did the rest, picking up a back-breaking first down. The Vikings would score a touchdown four plays later to put the game on ice.
Those plays were the difference between a competitive fourth quarter and a blowout.
Aaron Jones found his way into the end zone and did a Lambeau leap, which gave the Vikings a 27-10 lead against his former team in the fourth quarter.
Jones and Jordan Mason were solid if unspectacular for most of the game. Green Bay’s defense was good enough but did not make any significant plays against the run, either.
The final numbers were fine. The Packers gave up 106 yards on 27 carries to Minnesota’s running back tandem. They gave up 129 rushing yards total. That was not awful, but certainly not good enough.
Trey Smack missed another field goal. This one was from 53 yards and never had much of a chance. He’s missed nine kicks this year, which leads the league. The Packers are going to continue to ride the wave of a rookie kicker, but should they?
Ultimately, the loss of points did not matter on Sunday because the Packers’ offense could not do anything against Minnesota’s stingy defense, but it could matter in other games that play out this season.
The return game did little after Skyy Moore dropped out of the game with an ankle injury. J. Michael Sturdivant gave the ball away on a kick return in the fourth quarter. Meanwhile, Minnesota’s coverage was excellent and their kicker was automatic.
The third phase of the game was a decisive victory in Minnesota’s favor.
A lot of discussion is going to surround Matt LaFleur’s decision to give the Vikings an extra down in the first quarter. Minnesota was facing a third-and-8 when it was flagged for a facemask penalty. LaFleur’s options were to back the Vikings up 15 yards or allow them to kick a field goal from Green Bay’s 23.
LaFleur opted for a third-and-23 that put the Vikings back at the 38. Minnesota scored a touchdown on the next play.
From here, LaFleur made the right decision. Points are going to be at a premium against Minnesota’s defense, and Green Bay’s defense had played well up to that point. A sack would knock Minnesota out of field-goal range. An incompletion would have made the field goal harder to make.
Yes, the result was bad. The process, however, was good. A criticism of LaFleur is that he’s often too conservative. In that case, he’s coaching aggressively. Green Bay failing to execute in that situation falls on the players, not the coach.
“You got to roll the dice there and, certainly, that was a pivotal play in the game,” LaFleur said. “We can’t get beat in third-and-23. The odds of that are very, very low and they made us pay.”
The rest of the game? That’s fair to question. LaFleur did not seem interested in getting the ball out of his quarterback’s hands quickly as he was snowed under by Minnesota’s pressure packages.
“We’ve got to have better concepts to be able to get those balls out quicker,” Love said as part of a long answer about the pressure.
LaFleur and his offense found a little bit of rhythm in the second half by using some no huddle, but it was far too late by the time they made that adjustment.
Defensively, Jonathan Gannon’s defense did well to limit the damage from four takeaways to just three field goals but also didn’t take advantage of the Vikings playing…

title: Blame the Organization for Butt Whoopin’ Packers Were Handed by Vikings
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. – It takes every player on the field for a play to succeed.
It takes every player on the 53-man roster – heck, it takes all 70 on the team – to win a game.
It takes an entire organization to win a championship. Or not having a chance to win a championship.
The Green Bay Packers got sacked by the rival Minnesota Vikings on Sunday. All week, the players and coaches talked about how playing at Lambeau Field would help with the communication necessary to deal with the Vikings’ pressure packages. The Packers had a veteran offensive line, unlike the first game, and should have been prepared after getting blown out in the opener.
All of that was nonsense. Complete and utter garbage.
“That was a butt-whoppin’,” coach Matt LaFleur said to kick off his introductory remarks.
Yeah, it would be easy to blame the offensive line for missing blocks. It would be easy to blame LaFleur for expecting that game plan to win against that defense. It would be easy to blame quarterback Jordan Love for being skittish in the pocket.
And all those things would be true.
The reason for the loss, however, starts at the top with general manager Brian Gutekunst.
It’s Gutekunst’s complete and total mismanagement of the offense that has the team in its current predicament.
It was Gutekunst who used a first-round pick on left tackle Jordan Morgan in 2024, only to stunt his growth by having him play other positions for two seasons. It was Gutekunst who gave the bank to left guard Aaron Banks in 2025 for no good reason . It was Gutekunst who released Elgton Jenkins after shifting him to center following the signing of Banks. It was Gutekunst who drafted Anthony Belton in the second round in 2025. It was Gutekunst, realizing the errors in his ways, who went to a rummage sale to find Laken Tomlinson, Kevin Zeitler and Mekhi Becton when his offensive line got crushed to start the season.
In 2019, which was LaFleur’s first season as coach, the offensive line consisted of left tackle David Bakhtiari, left guard Elgton Jenkins, center Corey Linsley, right guard Billy Turner and right tackle Bryan Bulaga. That team reached the NFC Championship Game.
On Sunday, the line was Morgan at left tackle, Tomlinson at left guard, John Williams at center, Travis Glover at right guard and Belton at right tackle. It was the team’s sixth starting combination this season. With mediocre blocking, musical chairs and a lack of continuity, Green Bay has one foot on thin ice and another foot on a banana peel in the playoff race.
The Packers should have five big-ticket investments driving the line with Morgan at left tackle, Banks at center, Sean Rhyan at center, Belton at right guard and Zach Bako-Bewele at right tackle. Banks, Rhyan and Bako-Bewele were given big contracts to sign/re-sign in free agency and Morgan and Belton are premium draft picks.
It’s not Gutekunst’s fault, obviously, that Bako-Bewele is out with a major knee injury for the second consecutive year, but there is practically no evidence that any of the four other starters he selected are good enough to be playing for a championship contender.
Which is perhaps why the Vikings for the second time this season showed the world that the Packers aren’t really championship contenders.
On Sunday, Banks essentially was a healthy scratch other than a few snaps on special teams. Imagine that – the ninth-highest-paid guard in the NFL isn’t good enough to start on a team with a porous offensive line.
The Packers like the 34-year-old Tomlinson so much that they moved Banks to right guard. It’s a position he didn’t play at Notre Dame and hasn’t played in the NFL.
“We were going to shuffle up the O-line a little bit,” LaFleur explained after the game. “I think Laken’s been doing a pretty good job and we put him back to his natural position, and we were going to let Banks compete at the right guard. He doesn’t have a ton of time on task at that position, so we went the way we did tonight.”
Banks should be a bedrock on the line, a reliable pass protector and power blocker. Instead, he couldn’t even unseat Travis Glover, who had missed the last four games with a knee injury, to be a starter at right guard on Sunday. At left guard, he is behind Tomlinson, a past-his-prime lineman grabbed off a practice squad.
During a feeding-frenzy game against the Vikings, Banks was a $77 million backup.
Offensive lines need to be powering teams into the playoffs. This offensive line is powering the team into a ditch.
At this point, LaFleur and his coaches seem to be in the chucking-crap-at-a-wall-and-seeing-what-sticks phase of the season.
That’s not what championship teams do.
Things should improve once Rhyan returns to the lineup, potentially against the Rams following the make-believe bye week. However, it’s not as if Rhyan as the ninth-highest-paid center in the league was playing like he was the ninth-best center at the time of his ankle injury at Detroit.
The personnel problems have been exacerbated by the clown show of learning before every game which five blockers will play the five positions. Continuity seems like a punch line to a joke rather than a plan on the offensive line.
And to top it all off, LaFleur and Love seemed to be expecting the blockers to perform like Fordham’s famous Seven Blocks of Granite line, which included Vince Lombardi, rather than the Five Blocks of Swiss. To summarize the first half: Love dropped back to pass, the receivers ran downfield routes and Love got sacked.
Love was sacked five times in the first half, which tied for the most for any full game in the LaFleur era. The sack total swelled to eight through two-and-a-half quarters, tied for the most allowed by any team this season.
It was almost as if the Packers didn’t watch the success the Bills had with a quick passing game during their convincing win on Monday night at Minnesota last week.
“It’s obviously a bad decision, because our quarterback was getting abused just like he did in the first game,” LaFleur said. “We had called some of that early on, and it really wasn’t successful until the second half.”
Finally, the Packers pivoted and they almost got back in the game, which led to this remarkable combination of stats, with Love throwing quick (either by design or by necessity) and still getting pressure at a staggering level.
The Vikings defense pressured Jordan Love on 21 of 35 dropbacks (60.0%) and sacked him 8 times. Love faced a career-high pressure rate despite averaging 2.33 seconds to throw, his second-quickest time in a game. @MINvsGB | #Skol
“I think we had some success in the second half jumping the ball, doing some things, but I think to your point, when you’re facing a defense that’s pressuring that way, you’ve got to be able to get the ball out quick and have those answers and find the holes in the defense,” Love said.
Love noted the complexity and challenges of dealing with the Vikings' defensive front but also said the Vikings didn’t do anything they hadn’t seen on film during the week of prep. So, in other words, the linemen were not prepared mentally and overmatched physically.
“It’s missed opportunities, that’s all it is,” Love said, “and the conversations are what can we do better? What plays can we do better to get the ball out? Obviously, whatever we were calling right there was not working.”
No, it was not. Which begs the question of now what?
The players are the players and the coaches are the coaches. Help is not on the way. Gutekunst picked the blockers. LaFleur picked Luke Butkus to coach them.
Ultimately, Gutekunst handed LaFleur a pile of chicken feathers. With seven games remaining, starting with Myles Garrett, Aaron Donald and the Rams next week, and a daunting road ahead just to squeak into the playoffs, it’ll be up to LaFleur and Love to turn them into something other than the chicken crap the Packers drowned in on Sunday.
From an ugly defeat, @JacobWestendorf has his weekly winners and losers for the Packers. ⬇️…

title: Texans vs. Colts Thursday Night Football: How to Watch/Stream, Game Preview
full_text:
The Houston Texans are rallying for their Week 11 matchup against the Indianapolis Colts on a short week of preparation, as these two will have a primetime date on Thursday Night Football for their second meeting of the year.
The last time these two faced off, the Colts were the ones who got the edge, despite Houston dominating the turnover battle, 3-0–– which was the loss that ultimately dropped them to 0-3 after Week 3.
This week, the Texans simply can't afford to drop the ball again, as another loss would allow them to fall to 3-7, and might just be the nail in the coffin for their hopes of seeing their record make a comeback for a playoff run in the second half of the season.
Here's everything you need to know about the Texans' upcoming matchup against the Colts, including where to watch, betting lines, and more information:
All odds are provided by FanDuel Sportsbook .
Odds refresh periodically and are subject to change.
If you or someone you know has a gambling problem and wants help, call 1-800-GAMBLER.
Can the Texans' defense recover without Azeez Al-Shaair?: News surfaced this week of the Texans placing Pro Bowl linebacker Azeez Al-Shaair on injured reserve due to a groin injury that requires surgery. Houston's captain and green-dot signal caller will miss at least the next four weeks, and possibly more depending on how his recovery timeline looks. So can the Texans' defense rebound from such a loss? This game will be the second test to see whether or not they can do so. Henry To'oTo'o will act as Houston's new green-dot in the middle of the field–– according to DeMeco Ryans–– and Jake Hansen is likely to fill their other linebacker role. Time will tell if such a plan of attack will be enough.
How David Montgomery looks leading the backfield: Another name the Texans will be without in this game is their lead ball carrier in the running back room, Woody Marks, as he still sits in the middle of concussion protocol. But Houston will have David Montgomery in the lineup for the first time since Week 5. Montgomery hasn't performed particularly well when he's been on the field this season. He hasn't scored a touchdown since his hat trick performance in Week 1, and he's averaging just 2.7 yards per carry on the season. Expect to see him get a lot of work in the backfield against the Colts, but it remains to be seen how effective he looks with those extended opportunities.
Will Houston's penalty issues pop up once again?: It felt like the Texans' penalty issues had turned a corner in Week 9 against the LA Chargers as they incurred just six penalties for less than 40 yards en route to a dominant win. However, those concerns arose once again against the Browns as Houston recorded a whopping 13 penalties for over 100 yards given up. That's far from a recipe for success, and it's become a common trend for the Texans this season to fall into those frequent issues of lacking discipline and limiting flags. To ensure they can meet expectations for a one-sided victory against the Colts on Thursday, a large part of that relies on not getting behind so consistently when it comes to penalties.

title: With Marvin Harrison Jr. Out, Texans Will Lean on This WR vs. Colts
full_text:
The Houston Texans are heading into their Thursday Night Football matchup against the Indianapolis Colts without a key piece in their wide receiver room, as Marvin Harrison Jr. will miss his second straight game due to a hamstring injury he suffered ahead of Week 10's matchup vs. the Cleveland Browns.
And it's a less-than-ideal absence for the Texans to bear. It was around this time in the season where many would've expected Harrison Jr. to become a more frequently involved piece of Houston's offensive game plan and passing attack from when the team first traded for him.
But instead, they'll be forced to wait one more week before they get Harrison Jr. incorporated a bit further––which means against the Colts, the offense will have to rely on a few others to step up and make plays in the passing game in a must-win matchup against their AFC South rival.
So who might be the name to look towards in the Texans' offense as the most likely weapon to see more looks their way with one less wide receiver in the mix?
Of course, someone like Nico Collins is bound to get his fair share of looks ––as he did this past weekend against the Browns en route to his season-high 16 targets.
But outside of Collins and the targets he'll be due to see, the one name that I'll be keeping a close eye on in the wide receiver room set for a big day is none other than fourth-year veteran Xavier Hutchinson.
It's been nothing new for the Texans to keep Hutchinson involved as a big part of their weekly gameplan offensively, even when their receiving core is much healthier than it looks at the moment.
Since Week 1, Hutchinson has seen an average of over 60% of the Texans' offensive snaps, and has three games where he's recorded over 75% of the offensive snap share. Impressively, two of those games with over a 75% snap share have come in the last two weeks.
Hutchinson has been a reliable weapon for the Texans to lean on within a week-to-week basis as someone who can be a nice set of hands on the outside to move the chains as a short and intermediate target, and a positive blocker in the run game.
That's allowed him to stay on the field for long stretches, and that seems as if it could be the case once again this week against the Colts, knowing that Houston will continue to operate without Harrison Jr., as well as Jaylin Noel, who's been on injured reserve since the bye .
Last week against the Browns, the Texans handed Hutchinson a total of 51 snaps. That ultimately led to him seeing nine total targets (tying his season-high) and hauling in four catches for 51 yards and his third consecutive week of scoring a touchdown.
And for this game against the Colts, there's little to no reason as to why the Texans wouldn't be willing to give Hutchinson a big opportunity once again.
The wide receiver room is in need of a jolt in talent and production next to Collins. Hutchinson has proven to be a worthwhile piece of the receiver room–– even if not the most potent and explosive threat at the position–– and he fits the mold of an outside, versatile wideout that could be utilized in the snaps that Harrison Jr. leaves behind.
Again, when it comes to predicting who will lead the Texans' receiving corps in both targets and yards against the Colts, it's hard to circle anyone else outside of Nico Collins, simply based on how much of a featured part he was of Houston's offensive game plan last weekend.
But outside of Collins, it certainly wouldn't be shocking to see Hutchinson be next in line for those second-most targets.
That was the case for the Texans' passing offense against the Browns, and this week, as the personnel will be the same and following up from a solid performance from Hutchinson, the signs seem to be pointing towards another strong day on his behalf.
Of course, Tank Dell and Kayshon Boutte see their fair share of opportunities––as they have every week that they've been on the field this season––yet they might not get the same dose of snaps that Hutchinson has recently become accustomed to as of the last two weeks.

title: Texans Rule Out 4 Players on Final Injury Report for TNF vs. Colts
full_text:
The Houston Texans have released their third and final injury report of the week before they're tasked with a Thursday Night Football matchup against the Indianapolis Colts .
And based on those newly-released statuses, the Texans will be without at least four players for Thursday's action, while also having a couple more names who are deemed questionable leading up to kickoff.
Let’s take a look at what both the Texans and Colts are dealing with in terms of injuries rolling into their primetime matchup for Week 11:
RB Woody Marks (concussion) DE Danielle Hunter (hamstring) WR Marvin Harrison Jr. (hamstring) TE Brevin Jordan (foot/illness)
LB Jake Hummel (groin) OL Wyatt Teller (back)
As for who will be out for the Texans, there's a couple of key starters that will miss out on the action and certainly shift the game plan from Houston's normal setup.
For one, the Texans will be without Danielle Hunter for a second straight game , as the veteran pass-rusher has been dealing with a lingering hamstring injury dating back to last week's practice before facing the Cleveland Browns.
This will mark his second-ever missed game while being a part of the Texans, as he's had a full 17-game attendance in both 2024 and 2025. Without Hunter, it likely means that Jadeveon Clowney will claim the vast majority of snaps as Houston's second edge rusher opposite of Will Anderson Jr., who doesn't have an injury designation like he did heading into Week 10.
The Texans will also be without their leader in the backfield from the past four weeks, Woody Marks, as he still remains in concussion protocol from last week's game against the Browns and will miss his first game of the regular season.
The good news for the Texans, though, is that they will be able to get David Montgomery back in the lineup, who's been stuck on the sidelines with a groin injury dating back to Week 5's game against the Tennessee Titans.
Montgomery should be expected to claim the bulk of Houston's carries on Thursday, while Emari Demercado operates as the Texans' RB2 as he has for the last two weeks since he's been signed to the active roster.
The Texans will also be without Marvin Harrison Jr. for a second straight game with a hamstring injury, while Brevin Jordan will be missing as well with a foot injury/illness.
That'll take two weapons away from C.J. Stroud's arsenal on Thursday, but leave him with a receiving corps still headlined by Nico Collins, Tank Dell, Xavier Hutchinson, and Kayshon Boutte.
DT Jerry Tillery (calf) OL Jalen Travis (knee) CB Charvarius Ward (knee) OL Bernhard Raimann (concussion) TE Will Mallory (hamstring)

title: Texans' Key Matchups to Watch vs. Colts Include Nico Collins, Calen Bullock
full_text:
The Houston Texans have a pivotal game on the horizon on a short week against the Indianapolis Colts, as these two will be facing off for the second time this season on Thursday Night Football .
And this time, both teams have their backs against the wall with just three wins on the season and desperately need a victory on Thursday in order to keep any hopes of a late push to the postseason alive.
For the Texans to do just that, and also get revenge from their Week 3 loss against the Colts, they'll have to focus on a select few matchups that could dictate the result of this game, and take advantage of said battles.
Three matchups stick out more than the rest for this matchup, and deserve to be broken down a bit more to see just how the Texans can find their way to a fourth win on the season, and a bounce back performance from last weekend's loss to the Cleveland Browns .
With that in mind, let's take a look at three of the biggest matchups to watch for the Texans heading into their Week 11 matchup against their AFC South rival Colts:
When looking at the Colts' injury report, it's looking as if they could be without not just one, but both of their top corners on the boundary.
Sauce Gardner and Charvarius Ward have been listed as DNPs during the first two days of practice/walkthroughs, and seems to hint that Indianapolis might have to throw out a different look within their secondary against this Texans' passing attack.
Last week, it was slot specialist Justin Walley who took ahold of some of those snaps on the outside fo the Colts' secondary. And if that's the case again on Thursday against the Texans, there's a good chance that Nico Collins can go out and exploit that matchup in a big way.
Collins is coming off of one of his better performances of the season against the Cleveland Browns, where he saw a season-high 16 targets to convert that into nine catches, 94 yards, and a touchdown. Another game like that will make it a whole lot easier for Houston to consistently move the ball downfield, especially against a depleted Colts secondary.
The Colts' offense has struggled immensely when it comes to turnovers throughout the first half of the season, and a huge part of that blame can be placed on the shoulders of Daniel Jones. He's recorded a total of 17 turnovers over the course of Indianapolis' first 10 games of the season.
That creates a perfect opportunity for the Texans and their defense to take advantage of on Thursday night, and moreso within their secondary. Winning the turnover battle against this Colts offense is a must, considering how poor their ball security has been over the first half of the year.
And the name I'll be looking towards the most to try and generate those giveaways is Texans safety Calen Bullock, who currently leads Houston's defense in total interceptions on the year, combined with the fact that he just got his hands on an interception this past weekend against Deshaun Watson and the Browns.
Last time the Texans saw this Colts team and their offense, they won the turnover battle 3-0 and still came up short of a winning effort. This time, Houston will have to win that battle once again, but hope that it can result in chalking up a victory against this Indianapolis scoring attack that ranks 23rd in points scored and 29th in turnovers allowed.
The Texans' rushing defense has had its ups and downs over the course of this season.
Houston ranks just outside of the top 10 for total rushing yards allowed through the nine games they've played, but have had their fair share of lapses in games against the Jacksonville Jaguars, New York Giants, and LA Chargers, where they allowed over 100 total rushing yards on the day.
Ensuring that this week is not one of those games allowing 100 or more rushing yards will be extremely important to control the pace of the matchup. And knowing that the Texans have one of their toughest remaining matchups in terms of opposing running backs in Jonathan Taylor, it could be a task that's easier said than done.
The last time these two faced off , Taylor had a pretty quiet day for his standards. He had 23 carries for 68 yards, and had just one run that went off for 10 yards or more. A similar day on Taylor's behalf could be a huge lift to the Texans' chances of splitting their season series against this Colts team.

title: Where Texans' Playoff Odds Stand After Falling to 3-6
full_text:
The Houston Texans entered this season viewed as one of the NFL's safer bets to make the postseason.
After logging three straight playoff appearances and a Wild Card win in each , the writing felt like it was on the wall for the Texans to go and make another postseason run for 2026.
They had an elite defense on paper, an improved offense from the offseason, and a quarterback-head coach duo that has the necessary experience to seemingly make such a run possible for the fourth straight season.
But so far after 10 weeks, the Texans are far from in the driver's seat to make that fourth-consecutive postseason become a reality.
In fact, with their current record of 3-6 following this past weekend's loss to the Cleveland Browns , it projects to be a pretty steep uphill climb to make that playoff appearance actually happen.
No matter which way you look at it, the Texans currently project to be pretty comfortably on the outside looking in for the playoff picture in the AFC.
﻿ According to ESPN 's playoff odds via FPI , the Texans head into Week 11 with just a 31.2% chance of making the postseason.
To win the AFC South, those odds take a nosedive down to just 1.2%, considering the Jacksonville Jaguars sit four games ahead of Houston in the standings with just eight more weeks of action to go. The Texans have better odds to make the Super Bowl (1.6%) than they do to come out on top in the South.
Betting odds-wise, the outlook doesn't get much more appealing for the Texans. According to odds from FanDuel Sportsbook , Houston sits at +198 odds to make the postseason.
When stacked up against the rest of the conference, the Texans sit with the eighth-best odds to make the playoffs, sitting behind teams like the Cleveland Browns (-142) and the Pittsburgh Steelers (-300).
So is it impossible for the Texans to go on a run late in the season? Certainly not.
Actually, we saw Houston go on a similar run around this time last year when they rattled off nine straight wins after sitting at a 3-5 record after their Week 9 loss to the Denver Broncos ––and that also happened without their starting quarterback for three games.
Now, it certainly won't be easy for the Texans to repeat history here. Not only have they made things tougher on themselves by losing grip of some key head-to-head tiebreakers (against the Browns and the Bengals), but they'll also be dealing with a handful of impactful injuries over the coming weeks as well.
Azeez Al-Shaair was just placed on injured reserve to take him out for the next four weeks. Danielle Hunter is trending to miss his second straight game against the Indianapolis Colts. Even Houston's once-deep receiving core is slowly beginning to get more shallow without Jaylin Noel and Marvin Harrison Jr.
At the same time though, we know the talent that this Texans roster has around the building. Their defense has multiple Pro Bowlers, and the offense has been a step better than last year's product thanks to some C.J. Stroud heroics.
Pair that with a schedule that the Texans can take advantage of over the next few games against teams like the Colts, the Baltimore Ravens, and the Pittsburgh Steelers, and a nice three-game win streak could be exactly what Houston needs to breathe some life into their postseason hopes.
So while the Texans do have their work cut out for them in the weeks ahead if they want that postseason leap to come to fruition, they can't be totally counted out just yet.
If the next couple of games can swing in their favor, it could provide Houston the right amount of momentum that makes them a force that's too tough to stop in the second half of the season.
We've seen that be the case in 2025, and with a lot of the same pieces from that group still on the roster and the coaching staff, maybe history could be in line to repeat itself, despite many considering this Texans team to be dead in the water with a 3-6 record.

title: Texans Have Obvious Offensive Line Change to Make, But They Won't
full_text:
The Houston Texans' offensive line looked a tad bit different this past weekend against the Cleveland Browns.
In the midst of Keylan Rutledge's one-game absence due to a stinger that he suffered in Wednesday's practice, the Texans were forced to shuffle around their interior from their typical setup.
Rather than Rutledge settling in at left guard, the Texans decided to start fourth-round rookie Febechi Nwaiwu for his third-ever game in the league. Evan Brown and Ed Ingram took their usual spots at center and right guard, respectively.
So how did the adjusted Texans' offensive line perform?
Well, they've certainly seen better days . But it wasn't because of any lackluster performance from Nwaiwu.
In reality, outside of a costly fourth-quarter holding penalty, the rookie actually held his own by allowing just one total pressure on quarterback C.J. Stroud. The issues actually stemmed elsewhere around Houston's offensive front.
Where the Texans' offensive line really struggled was at their center position.
Starting center Evan Brown allowed six total pressures from the Browns' defensive line, by far the highest on Houston's offensive line throughout the day.
Texans OL pressures allowed today vs Cleveland via @SumerSports . Aireontae Ersery - 3 Febechi Nwaiwu - 1 Evan Brown - 6 Ed Ingram - 1 Trent Brown - 2 Stroud was pressured 22 times total with many of those being free rushers.
It's been a bit of a recurring theme for Brown to have left a little more to be desired on a weekly basis. Brown's 49.1 overall grade via Pro Football Focus on the season ranks 30th among 35 qualified centers, while his 45.7 run blocking grade ranks second-lowest among that same group.
Statistically, Brown has been a weak link on the Texans' offensive front throughout most of the season. He's incurred 11 total pressures and three penalties over the first nine games of the season, and was a sizable part of Houston's demise this past weekend against Cleveland to drop them to 3-6.
So where do the Texans go from here? Is there a better starting unit that the Texans could roll with that takes Brown out of the equation and creates an improved five-man front?
Well, one easy option the Texans could lean into to better their offensive line's production is to continue starting Nwaiwu––who performed well in his first-ever start this past weekend––while shifting Rutledge over to the center spot, who's expected to return from injury in Wek 11.
Rutledge was drafted earlier this year in the first round with the expectation that he could start as Houston's center from day one before he inevitably settled in as Houston's full-time left guard.
Rutledge spent most of his time playing right guard during his two previous seasons at Georgia Tech, but ran some center at the Senior Bowl and during the Texans' training camp to show that he's more than capable of having that necessary positional flexibility.
Such a move might give the Texans the necessary upside and security needed upfront for the second half of the season, while also moving off of a weak-link in Brown who has been a replacable-level center in the opportunities he's seen so far.
However, based on the latest presser from Texans head coach DeMeco Ryans, it seems the team has no plans of pivoting off of their regular five-man front from how they've looked for most of the season.
Ryan’s was asked during his Tuesday press conference before taking on the Indianapolis Colts in Week 11 about whether or not the team would consider any changes on the offensive line.
His response? He's expecting things to look no different than they have when the unit has been fully healthy this season.
"We're rolling with what we have right now," Ryans said of the offensive line. "Guys have done a good job. So we'll continue to keep going with that."
That means, rather than giving Nwaiwu a call-up for his second start on Thursday after a positive debut, Rutledge will be expected to fill back into his typical role as Houston's left guard, while Brown will continue to operate as their center.
Perhaps the Texans' offensive line at full health can have a bit more success against the Colts compared to their lowly performance from this past weekend in Cleveland . At least, that seems to be the hope from Houston's coaching staff.
Considering Houston allowed over a 54% pressure rate against the Browns, they'll have no choice but to improve on their offensive front if they want to find any sustained success moving into the second half of the year.
But if their offensive line continues to stumble in their next game against the Colts' defensive line that hasn't been too inspiring through the first 10 weeks of the season, the chatter surrounding a shake-up on their offensive front will only begin to get louder.
And if there was a shake-up to be made, Nwaiwu feels like the first guy who would get that promotion into their starting five-man front, and hope that he can provide the necessary spark to get this protection to a serviceable level.
For now, the Texans are rolling with the status quo. Only time will tell if such a decision to stand pat will pan out in their favor.

title: How Texans' Defense Will Adjust With Azeez Al-Shaair on Injured Reserve
full_text:
The Houston Texans' defense took a big hit heading into their Week 11 matchup against the Indianapolis Colts .
Pro Bowl linebacker Azeez Al-Shaair was placed on injured reserve due to a lingering groin injury . Al-Shaair missed this past weekend against the Cleveland Browns after missing last week's team practice, and now, he'll be set to miss the next four games as he recovers.
The Texans have placed Azeez Al-Shaair on the injured reserve list. Al-Shaair missed Week 10 against the Browns with a groin injury, and he’ll now be slated to miss the next 4 weeks. The earliest he can return will be in Week 15 vs. the Jaguars.
But the Texans not having Al-Shaair in the mix is a big loss for their overall defensive success. Al-Shaair is a captain, the green-dot signal caller, and an every-down player for Houston's defense. Not having him on the field for any stretch of time––let alone four weeks––is a significant loss.
So how might the Texans adjust now that Al-Shaair is set to miss multiple weeks, and who on their defense will be due for a bigger role now that he won't be a part of the equation until Week 15?
In terms of the personnel that the Texans will be running on a down-to-down basis, things won't be looking much different outside of taking Al-Shaair out of the equation.
We've seen the Texans make bigger shifts on their defense without someone like Jalen Pitre on the field, and instead run more 4-3 looks rather than their typical nickel sets. However, Houston probably won't be taking that approach without Al-Shaair on the field.
Instead, their defense will expect to look pretty similar to last week's setup: their regular nickel defense with five defensive backs and two linebackers on a down-to-down basis. But instead of Al-Shaair being on the field, Jake Hansen will be in line to take his snaps as their middle linebacker.
Last weekend against the Browns without Al-Shaair on the field, it was Hansen who took ahold of 97% of the Texans' total defensive snaps , only coming off for two plays over the course of the day. Henry To'oTo'o took ahold of 100% of the defensive snaps.
When Al-Shaair missed Week 4 against the Dallas Cowboys, the setup was similar for the Texans and their defensive personnel . Hansen claimed 95% of their defensive snaps, but then-practice squad call-up Kenneth Murray was deemed their green dot signal-caller and saw over 80% of the defensive snaps.
Moving forward, though, it's easy to imagine that Hansen will be the Texans' new green-dot signal caller for the extent that Al-Shaair is out of the picture.
Kenneth Murray is still a part of Houston's practice squad, but with all three of his call-ups used on the season, he'd have to be signed to the 53-man roster to be on the gameday roster once again; something that hasn't happened to this point.
So moving forward, you can expect the Texans' defensive personnel to more than likely consist of Hansen and To'oTo'o leading the way. Murray also remains a name to keep on the radar, but only if Houston decides to ink him to a traditional contract for the 53-man roster.
Will that be enough to keep the Texans' defense afloat while shorthanded? It's tough to say. Houston's defense has been underwhelming this season with Al-Shaair on the field, and Hansen didn't perform much better in Week 10 when he saw an increase in opportunities.
Hansen allowed over 100 yards and eight catches on the 10 plays he was targeted against the Browns; the most of any player on the Texans' defense. Houston will have to be better in coverage moving forward, and a large part of that relies on Hansen's ability to keep the middle of the field in check.
Time will tell if the Texans can hold things together without their defensive leader, because for the next four weeks, they have no choice but to move forward with him out of the picture.

title: Texans Get Brutal Update on LB Azeez Al-Shaair's Lingering Injury
full_text:
The Houston Texans just announced a pretty concerning update regarding the injury status of Pro Bowl linebacker Azeez Al-Shaair.
According to the Texans, Al-Shaair has been placed on injured reserve ahead of Houston's Week 11 game against the Indianapolis Colts.
Al-Shaair was on the Texans' injury report dating back to last week's game against the Cleveland Browns , which led to him missing all three days of practice and being ruled out for Sunday's action.
And now, it appears that Al-Shaair's absence will linger much longer than just that Week 10 game against Cleveland.
Per Jonathan M. Alexander of the Houston Chronicle , Al-Shaair's groin injury is one that is deemed “significant" and will require surgery.
Azeez Al-Shaair's groin injury is one that is significant and requires surgery, per a source. He's not been ruled out for the season, though.
Al-Shaair has been dealing with the same groin injury that's now placed him on injured reserve dating back to Week 3 against the Indianapolis Colts .
That injury led to him missing the following week against the Dallas Cowboys, but then returned in Week 5 against his former team, the Tennessee Titans. But now, he'll be forced to miss a little more time with that same issue.
Al-Shaair has yet to be ruled out for the remainder of the season. Yet, at the very least, he'll be due to miss around a month simply because of his status on injured reserve.
Al-Shaair's injured reserve designation will keep him out for the next four weeks at a minimum: against the Colts, the Baltimore Ravens, the Pittsburgh Steelers, and the Washington Commanders.
His first chance to return to the lineup comes in Week 15 against the Jacksonville Jaguars in the event he's only sidelined for the minimum four weeks that come with an injured reserve placement. However, it remains to be seen just how quickly his rehab process will go in the weeks ahead.
Al-Shaair, while he hasn't been up to the same standard this season that he was during his Pro Bowl campaign of 2025, is still a critical component of the Texans' defensive success when he's healthy and on the field.
In the seven games that he's played this season, Al-Shaair has put together 68 total tackles, one tackle for loss, and three passes defended. He currently leads the Texans' defense in combined tackles, and ties for third in solo tackles behind only Calen Bullock and Kamari Lassiter.
The Texans will now be forced to adjust on their defense in the weeks ahead without Al-Shaair. And in all likelihood, their starting linebackers will look pretty similar to what they rolled out this past weekend against the Browns while he was ruled out.
Jake Hansen was elevated to start next to Henry To'oTo'o within the Texans' front seven, just as he did when Al-Shaair was out for Week 4 against the Cowboys.
In the weeks ahead, Hansen could be in line to be Houston's starting middle linebacker, or at least until Al-Shaair is ready to return to the field. Fourth-round rookie Wade Woodaz could also have a route to getting more reps on the defensive side of the ball as well.
Regardless, being without Al-Shaair––one of the Texans' team captains and their green dot on the defense––is a devastating loss for the success on that side of the ball as a whole.
We'll see how Houston winds up performing without him, but there's no doubt that his absence makes the climb out of their 3-6 hole a whole lot tougher than it would be with him as a part of the equation.

title: What to Expect From the Texans' Backfield vs. Colts on TNF
full_text:
The Houston Texans' backfield is setting up to look a bit different than usual heading into their Week 11 matchup vs. the Indianapolis Colts.
During the Texans' latest contest against the Cleveland Browns this past weekend, Houston's lead in the backfield, Woody Marks, wound up suffering a concussion that would lead to him leaving the game in the third quarter, and thus be put in concussion protocol for the week ahead.
And on a short week before facing the Colts on Thursday Night Football, there's little to no chance that Marks will be able to give it a go . Concussion protocol typically takes one to two weeks for players to clear, and with only a few days of preparation, Marks won’t have much of a lengthy timeline to bank on.
So what can we expect from the Texans' running back room heading into Week 11 without Marks in the picture? Let's break the situation down.
While the Texans have been without their veteran counterpart to Marks, David Montgomery, dating back to Week 5 against the Tennessee Titans, signs continue to point towards his return to the field coming as soon as this week against the Colts.
Montgomery was a full participant in the Texans' team practice on Friday before facing the Browns, and was deemed a full participant during Houston's walkthrough on Monday ahead of their Thursday Night Football matchup.
While his participation during the Texans' upcoming two practices will be a better indicator of whether or not he'll be able to play, a couple more full participations would be a pretty solid sign that his return will be in play for Week 11.
And if that's the case, you can expect Montgomery to claim a vast majority of the Texans' work in the backfield, perhaps just simply taking the role that Marks has when healthy; someone logging around 16 rushes per game, gets work in the passing game, and is on the field for upwards of 70% of the offensive snaps.
If Montgomery is good to go and Marks is out, that places Emari Demercado in line to take the Texans' RB2 role, just as he has for the past couple of weeks that he's been signed while Montgomery has been sidelined.
Through the past two games, Demercado has seen an average 27% snap share on the offensive end, along with 6.5 carries and one reception per game.
So while Montgomery claims about three-fourths of the reps in the backfield, and most of the work on the goal line, Demercado will likely claim the remainder as a change-of-pace back, and still get his fair share of opportunities.
With just three running backs on the active roster, and one of those in Marks likely not suiting up for Thursday, it puts the Texans in a situation where they'll be best served to bring another running back onboard for this game against the Colts, even if just a short-term depth plug-in.
And the name who makes the most sense to be that short-term depth option is Dare Ogunbowale, who was cut from the active roster earlier last week as the team signed Nikko Remigio to the 53-man, but was then re-signed to the practice squad in time for their matchup against the Colts.
Considering the Texans still have two more call-ups to use on Ogunbowale as a part of the practice squad, it would make sense for Houston to use one more of those for Week 11 while Marks is absent, and give Ogunbowale work as a part of their special teams unit, with a few looks on the offensive end as well.
Over the past three weeks, the Texans have given Ogunbowale an average of 10 offensive snaps per game, but have only given him one carry and two receptions over those appearances. Expect more of the same this week, in the event he is indeed called up from the practice squad.

title: Why Colts Fans Should Value TNF Matchup Over GTA VI Release
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts and Houston Texans could not have picked a worse primetime game to play in.
This AFC South matchup would be appointment viewing if both teams were in the hunt for playoff contention; however, with the Colts being 3-7 and the Texans being 3-6, there's almost no reason for non-fans to tune in.
Sure, two evenly matched teams, even if they're both subpar units compared to the rest of the league, could make for a fun time, but this time around is much, much different.
Not only does this matchup have the potential to rival the infamous 2022 Thursday Night Football showdown between the Indianapolis Colts and Denver Broncos, a game whose scores were exclusively comprised of field goals, but it comes on the same day as one of the most highly anticipated days in recent memory: the official release of Grand Theft Auto VI .
The long-awaited arrival of Rockstar Studios' most recent installment of their world-famous video game series, Grand Theft Auto (GTA), is set to be the biggest release in video game history.
This gaming series is one of the most well-known franchises to date, and there's a legitimate chance that this Thursday's AFC South matchup could be the sport's least-watched primetime game in NFL history because of it.
That may seem hyperbolic, given how the league has only continued to grow, netting unforeseen exposure in the form of an international fanbase.
Surely diehard football fans will at least throw the game in question on in the background as they navigate the new-and-improved Vice City, but it won't be enough to compete with.
Grand Theft Auto VI does have one barrier to entry that the NFL does not: being an M-rated game.
Just like moviegoing, gamers must be at least 17 years old if they want to purchase an M-rated product, according to the ESRB Ratings Guide . However, times have changed drastically.
Nowadays, video game companies are doing away with physical media and are becoming fully virtual. That means anyone can purchase an M-rated game, so long as their gaming account says they're of age.
The NFL is for all ages, and that definitely gives it an advantage, but the 13-year wait for Grand Theft Auto VI has garnered the most hype that any medium has in recent memory, so much so that news sites are predicting a net loss for the economy, given how many people are expected to call off work to be part of the once-in-a-lifetime event.
That's definitely a stretch, kind of, but it will play at least some part.
This day will potentially go down in history as the last video game to earn such hype, but when it comes to Indianapolis Colts fans, this could be the turning point that finally points them in the right direction.
With that being said, let's get into why exactly the Colts' fanbase should take a few hours to watch their team, despite the result of said game likely not mattering much in the grand scheme of things.
The Indianapolis Colts' 2026-27 season is lost. There's no denying that.
Following general manager Chris Ballard's firing, Indianapolis Colts principal owner and CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon has traded away multiple longtime key contributors, leaving the franchise devoid of veteran talent for the first time in a long time.
Yes, the former Colts in question ultimately didn't do enough to get the job done, but they still carried some serious talent, and now Indianapolis is left with unproven pieces.
However, those young pieces in question have recently been coming into their own , and it has made the Colts' outlook all the more promising.
It's still a bleak outlook, especially considering the Colts don't have a franchise quarterback to usher in the new era with, nor do they possess a first-round pick in the upcoming draft, but the trajectory is improving with each passing week.
When it comes to their primetime matchup against the Houston Texans, both teams are missing key starters , making the overall matchup that much more uninspiring.
The Colts will be without their veteran cornerback Charvarius Ward Sr., and potentially Sauce Gardner (calf), as well as both tackles in Bernhard Raimann and Jalen Travis, against the Texans. Although this may seem like even more reason not to tune in as a Colts fan, there's reason to believe it'll help them out in the long run.
Second-year cornerback Justin Walley, aka the reigning AFC Defensive Player of the Week, will get his chance to serve as the Colts' CB1, or at least CB2. This is intriguing on its own, but couple the fact that fellow rookie Kapena Gushiken and Johnathan Edwards could get more run as well.
Furthermore, the Colts also recently designated starting linebacker Jaylon Carlies to injured reserve. Veteran linebacker and Week 1 starter Akeem Davis-Gaither also remains on injured reserve, meaning that the rookie duo of CJ Allen and Bryce Boettcher will be a starting tandem for the first time in their young careers.
Third-year offensive lineman Matt Goncalves will likely slide back out to right tackle to replace Jalen Travis, while veteran tackle Luke Tenuta is set to fill in for Bernhard Raimann as Daniel Jones' blindside protector.
Speaking of which, Daniel Jones will likely be the sole reason that some Colts fans refuse to tune in, given that he's played like the worst starting quarterback in the NFL this season (league-leading 12 interceptions), but this could very well be the beginning of something great: not only GTA's release, but Jones' inevitable demise.
Nobody should ever root for someone's failure, but the Colts are losing valuable reps with Jones manning the charge.
Colts' head coach Shane Steichen should've benched Jones weeks ago, but another unacceptable performance this week could be the final nail in the coffin that brings Anthony Richardson or Riley Leonard in to finish the season.
Regardless of how things turn out tonight, Colts fans should give their team a chance to prove they deserve their time.
Noah Compton is the Publisher of Indianapolis Colts On SI. Noah is from the Indy area and has been covering the Colts since 2022, including stops at FanSided, The Blue Stable, and SBNation.

title: Week 11 Injury Report: Colts, Texans Each Without Key Veterans for Thursday Night Football
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts and Houston Texans are preparing for an important AFC South matchup on Thursday Night Football, with both teams looking to navigate the challenges of a short week.
Injuries could play a significant role in how the divisional showdown unfolds, with plenty to keep an eye on prior to kickoff. Here's a complete look at the latest injury updates for both teams, including player designations and potential implications for the matchup.
Indianapolis Colts Final Injury Report
The biggest concern for Indianapolis heading into Thursday night's matchup is the state of its offensive line. The Colts will be without both starting tackles in Bernhard Raimann and Jalen Travis.
Raimann's absence is also significant after he exited Sunday's win over Miami with a concussion. Luke Tenuta replaced him at left tackle and is in line for another start against Houston. Matt Goncalves had to kick out from right guard to right tackle last week, where he played in college, and the Colts slotted Dalton Tucker in at guard next to him. That's likely the same route Indianapolis will take on Thursday night, especially with Charlie Heck listed as questionable.
The secondary could be facing an equally significant challenge. Charvarius Ward has been ruled out with a knee injury, while Sauce Gardner remains questionable after picking up a calf injury against the Dolphins. Gardner's availability will be one of the biggest things to monitor ahead of kickoff, particularly given the talented wide receivers on the Texans roster, mainly Nico Collins.
The absence of Jerry Tillery will further thin Indianapolis' defensive tackle rotation for the second straight week. Tillery leaves additional responsibilities for Grover Stewart, Adetomiwa Adebawore and Kevin Givens. The only defensive tackle on the practice squad is Cam Ball, an undrafted free agent who could easily get a call-up on gameday.
Anthony Gould and Luke Rhodes are both questionable, creating some uncertainty at wide receiver and long snapper, respectively. Rhodes would miss his second straight game should he be unable to go, being replaced by Jacob Bobenmoyer for the evening. Indianapolis is fairly healthy at wide receiver, but given the lack of consistent production in that group, missing any player would be a big deal, including Gould.
Ultimately, Gardner is the name to monitor between now and kickoff, as the Colts missing their top two cornerbacks would spell disaster for their defense against a passing offense that's been clicking over the last few weeks.
Houston Texans Injury Report
Houston will be without one of its most important defensive players Thursday night, as defensive end Danielle Hunter has been ruled out with a hamstring injury. Hunter has been a major part of the Texans' pass rush, and his absence should give Indianapolis' already-depleted offensive line one less player to worry about. That said, Will Anderson Jr. has already eclipsed double-digit sacks on the season, so Indianapolis' offensive line will still have their hands full.
The Texans will also be without wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr., who has been sidelined throughout the week with a hamstring injury. His absence leaves Houston without another option in its receiving corps, although Tank Dell has avoided a game designation after practicing fully all three days and is in line to play.
Running back Woody Marks and tight end Brevin Jordan were both also ruled out. Marks' absence could mean a larger workload for David Montgomery, who practiced fully throughout the week and carries no game designation after dealing with a groin injury.
Houston has three additional players listed as questionable, including cornerback Jaylin Smith, linebacker Jake Hummel and guard Wyatt Teller. Teller's availability is worth monitoring given the importance of maintaining continuity along the offensive line. Smith and Hummel could also affect Houston's defensive depth, although neither carries the same significance as Hunter's absence.
Overall, Hunter's absence is the biggest development on Houston's report, particularly given the Colts' offensive line concerns. Indianapolis will have an opportunity to take advantage of his absence, but Anderson and the rest of Houston's defensive front remain capable of creating problems.
On the other side of the football, Montgomery's availability provides some relief for a Texans offense losing Marks, while Dell avoiding a game designation is another positive development for Houston heading into the divisional matchup.

title: Colts Rookie Report: More Opportunities Arising for Several Draft Picks
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts are entering the final stretch of the 2026 season, and their rookie class has experienced a variety of different developments along the way. Some players have established themselves as regular contributors, while others are still working to carve out their respective roles.
With Indianapolis looking toward the future, the remaining games will be especially important for evaluating the team's young talent. Several rookies have already taken on larger roles, providing the Colts with a better understanding of what they have moving forward.
Here's a look at how Indianapolis' rookies have performed through 10 games of the 2026 season.
CJ Allen's rookie season has taken a positive turn over the last several weeks. After dealing with injuries that limited his availability early in the year, the second-round pick has found his footing and established himself as the new leader of the Indianapolis defense, likely for years to come.
Allen has recorded 34 tackles, two tackles for loss, and two sacks across seven games (three starts). His first career start against the Jacksonville Jaguars was particularly encouraging , as he finished with a team-high 10 tackles, a tackle for loss, and his first NFL sack.
Since then, Allen has only gotten better. He followed up his performance in Jacksonville with anouther double-digit tackle performance against the Dallas Cowboys. Sunday's matchup with the Miami Dolphins proved to be his most complete yet, finishing with nine tackles, a pass defended, a game-sealing sack and an interception that was called back due to a penalty.
It took a little while for Allen to fully kick things into gear, but now that he's playing consistently, he's improving with every passing week . The Colts absolutely have found a player they can build around on defense going forward.
AJ Haulcy has had a difficult introduction to the NFL despite earning the starting strong safety job alongside Cam Bynum coming out of training camp.
The Colts' third-round pick has been a regular presence in the Indianapolis secondary, starting nine games, but his performance hasn't necessarily justified the consistent playing time. His 43.4 overall grade from Pro Football Focus ranks 96th among 100 qualified safeties.
The coverage concerns have been particularly evident, with Haulcy allowing a 137.5 passer rating when targeted and recording just one pass breakup. He's also been credited with nine missed tackles, giving him plenty of areas to address as he adjusts to the professional level.
Haulcy has shown some flashes throughout his rookie campaign, but the overall numbers paint a difficult picture. There's still plenty of time for him to acclimate to the NFL game, but the early returns on investment haven't been great for Indianapolis.
Jalen Farmer has gradually worked his way into a larger role along the Colts' offensive line after beginning his rookie season as a reserve.
The Colts' fourth-round pick out of Kentucky made his first career start against Jacksonville following the Quenton Nelson trade, and his transition hasn't been without some growing pains. Per Pro Football Focus , Farmer has yet to allow a sack, but holds a pass blocking grade of only 41.8.
Bengals on both sides of the ball in the Week 10 Team of the Week! 🐅 pic.twitter.com/6CdxXk6pTf
There have been some encouraging signs recently, though. Farmer put together his best performance of the season against Miami, earning an 83.8 overall PFF grade that ranked third among all NFL guards in Week 10, good enough to make the Pro Football Focus Team of the Week.
The Colts are still figuring out what they have in their young offensive lineman, but his recent improvement is an encouraging development as he continues adjusting to the NFL level.
Bryce Boettcher has started to earn a larger role in the Colts' linebacker rotation as the season has progressed. The fourth-round pick out of Oregon has appeared in eight games, making four starts, and has taken advantage of increased opportunities with Akeem Davis-Gaither sidelined. Boettcher recorded a season-high 12 tackles against Dallas before following that performance with seven more against Miami. His 44 total tackles are encouraging, though there is still plenty of room for development.
Boettcher has been considerably more effective against the run, earning a 53.8 run-defense grade compared to a 36.0 coverage grade. He also recorded an 87.4 run-defense grade against Miami, the highest mark among Indianapolis defenders in the game. His limitations in coverage remain an area to improve, but the rookie has shown that he can hang with the big boys.
With Davis-Gaither and Jaylon Carlies both on injured reserve for at least the next four games, more opportunities are coming Boettcher's way. If he can take advantage of the opportunity, he could have a longer-term future with the Colts than one might think.
George Gumbs Jr. has had a relatively quiet start to his NFL career, largely due to limited opportunities in a crowded Indianapolis defensive front. The fifth-round pick out of Florida was always going to be a bit of a project at first, but he has appeared in six games so far. He has yet to record a sack or make a significant impact statistically, recording only four total tackles and two quarterback pressures.
Gumbs is still a developmental piece for the Colts, and there isn't much to evaluate given his limited playing time. With several veterans ahead of him on the depth chart, his immediate opportunities may remain limited, but the remaining games should provide another chance to get the rookie some valuable experience.
Caden Curry has become one of the more intriguing developments among Indianapolis' rookie class. He's had a relatively slow start to his NFL career, but his role began to expand considerably in the middle of the season.
Curry recorded his first career sack against Dallas in Week 9, adding a fumble recovery after also recovering a fumble against Jacksonville the previous week. He's now up to 23 tackles, one sack and two fumble recoveries through 10 games.
Curry's recent production is encouraging, particularly considering how limited his opportunities were early in the season. However, his playing time took a hit against Miami following Arden Key's return from injured reserve, as the sixth-round pick played just 13 defensive snaps. The Colts have several established players ahead of him along the defensive line, but Curry has shown enough in recent weeks to warrant continued opportunities.
His development will be worth monitoring as Indianapolis evaluates its young defensive front.
Seth McGowan has arguably been the most productive offensive rookie on Indianapolis' roster this season. The seventh-round running back has steadily earned more opportunities in the Colts' backfield, proving to be a valuable complement to Jonathan Taylor.
Through 10 games, McGowan has rushed for 285 yards and two touchdowns on 55 carries, averaging an impressive 5.2 yards per attempt. He's also forced 11 missed tackles, showcasing the physical running style that has made him an effective option when given opportunities.
McGowan is coming off his best performance yet , rushing for 77 yards and a touchdown on just 12 carries in Sunday's victory over Miami. He averaged 6.4 yards per attempt and consistently made the most of his opportunities, while also setting new career highs in carries and rushing yards.
Taylor will remain the focal point of the Colts' backfield, but McGowan has done more than enough to establish himself as a promising piece of Indianapolis' future at running back.
Deion Burks hasn't had many opportunities to make an impact during his rookie season, spending much of the first half of the year buried on Indianapolis' wide receiver depth chart.
His outlook could look considerably different over the second half of the season , however.
